guides.title: Plywood, MDF and Sheet Goods Explained
guides.summary: A practical guide to plywood, MDF, particleboard, OSB and hardboard: how each panel is made, how to read grades and stamps, which panel suits which job, and how to cut, join, edge, finish, store and handle full sheets safely.
guides.safetyNote: Working with sheet goods involves real hazards. Circular saws and table saws can kick back a panel with enough force to cause serious injury; always support sheets fully, keep blades sharp, use a riving knife or splitter on the table saw, and never reach over a running blade. Cutting and sanding MDF and particleboard produces very fine dust that irritates lungs and eyes, and the urea-formaldehyde resins in many panels release formaldehyde, which is classified as a human carcinogen; cut outdoors or with dust extraction, and wear a properly fitted respirator (N95 minimum, P100 preferred) plus eye and hearing protection. A full sheet of 3/4-inch MDF weighs roughly 95 pounds; lift with a helper or panel carrier, and store sheets so they cannot tip onto anyone. Glues, solvents and finishes need ventilation; follow the label.

sections.heading: What Sheet Goods Are and Why Panels Exist
sections.body:
Sheet goods are engineered wood panels manufactured in large, flat, uniform sheets, most commonly 4 by 8 feet, about 1220 by 2440 millimeters, in thicknesses from 1/8 inch hardboard up to 1-1/8 inch structural subfloor. The family includes plywood in its many grades, medium-density fiberboard or MDF, particleboard and its melamine-faced cousins, oriented strand board or OSB, and hardboard. What unites them is that each takes wood apart, into veneers, strands, chips or individual fibers, and reassembles it with adhesive under heat and pressure into a panel with properties solid lumber cannot offer: great width without gluing up boards, uniformity from sheet to sheet, and, above all, dimensional stability.

Stability is the heart of the matter. Solid wood is a bundle of straws: it barely moves along its length but shrinks and swells substantially across the grain as humidity changes, on the order of a quarter inch across a 12-inch-wide flatsawn board between a dry winter interior and a humid summer. Every traditional furniture joint, from the frame-and-panel door to the sliding dovetail, exists to manage that movement. Engineered panels largely cancel it. Plywood crosses each veneer's grain against its neighbors so each layer restrains the next; fiber and particle panels randomize the wood elements so movement is small and equal in every direction. The result is a panel you can screw down at its edges, veneer, laminate or paint, and expect to stay flat and the same size in January and July. That is why cabinet boxes, drawer bottoms, door skins, wall sheathing and floor decks are all panel products today.

The economics matter as much as the engineering. A tree yields far more usable material peeled into veneer or flaked into strands than sawn into clear boards, because knots and defects that would ruin lumber simply get distributed or cut around. Fast-growing small-diameter trees, aspen, southern pine, plantation eucalyptus, that could never yield wide clear boards make excellent OSB and fiber panels. Sheet goods thus track a century of forestry: as old-growth clear lumber grew scarce and expensive, industry learned to build better wood from worse trees. Softwood plywood was the great construction panel of the mid twentieth century; OSB, commercialized in the early 1980s, overtook plywood in North American sheathing by around 2000 because it delivers comparable structural performance from cheaper fiber.

Each panel type is a different point on a set of trade-off curves: strength and stiffness per pound, screw-holding, water resistance, surface quality, flatness, ease of machining, and price. Plywood is the strongest and most water-tolerant but the most expensive and the least perfectly flat. MDF is the flattest and smoothest, machines like hardwood, and is the cheapest route to painted work, but it is heavy, weak in screw-holding at edges, and hates water. Particleboard is cheaper still and serves under plastic laminate and melamine. OSB wins on structural cost. Hardboard covers the thin-panel jobs. Learning sheet goods is learning to match those curves to the job in hand, and the rest of this guide works through the family one panel at a time, then turns to the practical craft of cutting, joining, edging, finishing and storing them.

sections.heading: How Plywood Is Made: Veneers, Plies and Cross-Graining
sections.body:
Plywood is made by gluing thin sheets of wood, called veneers or plies, in a stack with the grain direction of each layer running at right angles to its neighbors. The log, called a peeler, is first debarked and usually soaked or steamed to soften it. It is then mounted in a giant lathe and spun against a full-length knife, which peels a continuous ribbon of veneer the way paper unrolls from a roll, a process called rotary cutting. Veneer thickness typically runs from about 1/40 inch for faces to 1/8 inch and more for cores. The ribbon is clipped into sheets, sorted for defects, dried to a few percent moisture content, and patched where knots fell out. Face-quality veneers for hardwood plywood may instead be sliced from a flitch rather than rotary-peeled, because slicing produces the straight, repeating figure of sawn lumber, while rotary peeling produces a broad, wild, watery figure; this is why cheap birch plywood looks swirly and premium plain-sliced walnut plywood looks like boards.

The assembled sandwich almost always contains an odd number of plies, three, five, seven and up, so that the two outer faces both run the long direction of the sheet and the construction is balanced around a central ply. Balance is critical: every layer on one side of the center must be mirrored in thickness, species and grain direction on the other side, because an unbalanced panel bows as humidity changes, one side pulling harder than the other. This is also why you should finish or laminate both faces of a panel the same way; sealing one face and leaving the other bare unbalances moisture exchange and can cup a previously flat sheet.

Glue is spread on the crossband veneers, the stack is laid up, pressed cold to tack it, then hot-pressed at roughly 250 to 300 degrees Fahrenheit under hundreds of pounds per square inch while the thermosetting resin cures. Interior panels traditionally used urea-formaldehyde resin; structural and exterior panels use phenol-formaldehyde, the dark red-brown glue line you can see on the edge of construction plywood, which is essentially waterproof once cured. The pressed panels are trimmed to final size, sanded if the grade calls for it, graded, stamped and strapped into units.

Cross-graining is what gives plywood its character. Wood is roughly twenty times stronger along the grain than across it, and it moves across the grain but not along it. Alternating the grain at ninety degrees each layer means the panel is strong and stable in both directions: each ply's weak direction is reinforced by its neighbors' strong direction, and each ply's urge to shrink across its grain is resisted by the plies glued to it. The panel is still somewhat stronger and stiffer along its face grain, which usually runs the 8-foot length, a fact that matters when you orient shelves or sheathing. Cross-graining also means plywood holds screws and nails far better than fiber panels, resists splitting, and can be worked with ordinary edge joints. Its costs are the visible striped edge, the possibility of internal voids where core knots fell out, and thickness that runs slightly under nominal, a 3/4-inch panel is typically 23/32 inch, because sanding removes material, a detail that matters the first time you cut a dado to a nominal dimension and find the shelf rattling.

sections.heading: Reading Plywood Grades and Stamps
sections.body:
Every stack of plywood at the lumberyard is speaking to you in a compact code, and reading it saves money in both directions, not paying for quality you do not need, and not building failure into a project with a panel that was never rated for the job. For North American softwood construction plywood, the system to know is the APA, the Engineered Wood Association, whose grade stamp appears on the back or edge of rated panels. Face and back veneers are graded by letter. A is smooth and paintable, with only small, neatly made repairs. B allows tight knots to about an inch and repair patches. C allows knots to roughly 1-1/2 inches, knotholes to about an inch, and splits; C-plugged is a C face with the open defects patched. D, allowed only in interior-rated panels, permits larger knots and knotholes. A panel is named by its two faces: AC has one good face and one knotty face, and is the standard choice where one side shows; BC is a workhorse utility panel; CDX is the rough construction staple. The X does not mean exterior panel; it means exterior glue, phenolic adhesive that tolerates weather exposure during construction, on a panel whose veneers are C and D grade.

The stamp carries more than letters. Exposure ratings state moisture tolerance: Exterior panels have waterproof glue and veneer grades fit for permanent weather exposure; Exposure 1 panels have the same waterproof glue but lower-grade veneers, rated to shrug off construction delays and rain before the building is dried in, not to live outdoors forever. Sheathing stamps include a span rating that looks like a fraction, such as 32/16: the left number is the maximum recommended support spacing in inches when the panel is used as roof sheathing, the right when used as subflooring. Sturd-I-Floor panels, made for single-layer floors, carry a single span number and usually tongue-and-groove edges. You will also see the panel's thickness, mill number and the standard it meets, PS 1 for veneered structural plywood.

Hardwood and decorative plywood uses a different vocabulary. Faces are graded A through E or by descriptive terms, and backs by numbers 1 through 4, so a cabinet shop might order A1 maple for exposed ends and C2 for hidden carcass parts. The face species named is only the face; the core underneath is a separate question covered in the next section. Matching terms describe how the face veneer leaves are arranged: book-matched leaves mirror each other like an opened book, slip-matched leaves repeat side by side, and rotary-cut whole-piece faces have the broad wild figure of peeled veneer. Imported panels follow their own conventions; Baltic birch, for instance, is commonly graded B, BB, CP and C, with B the cleanest single-piece face and BB allowing small oval patches.

Two cautions round out stamp-reading. First, grade describes appearance and rating, not flatness or void content, and quality within a grade varies a great deal by mill and country of origin; inspect actual sheets, sight down the length for bow and twist, and look at the edges for core gaps. Second, formaldehyde emissions are their own certification: panels sold in the United States must comply with the CARB Phase 2 and federal TSCA Title VI limits, and stamps or stickers will say so, with terms like NAF, no added formaldehyde, and ULEF, ultra-low-emitting formaldehyde, marking the cleanest resin systems, worth seeking for interior cabinetry and anyone sensitive to the gas.

sections.heading: Construction Plywood: Sheathing, Subfloor and CDX
sections.body:
Construction plywood is the structural skin of the wood-framed building. Nailed over studs, joists and rafters, rated panels do three jobs at once: they carry loads across the spaces between framing members, they brace the frame against racking from wind and earthquake, turning a floppy rectangle of studs into a rigid shear wall, and they provide the nail base for roofing, siding and flooring above. The panels are almost always softwood, Douglas fir and southern yellow pine dominating in North America, with veneer grades C and D and waterproof phenolic glue, because nothing about the job requires a pretty face and everything about it requires strength, stiffness, nail-holding and tolerance of getting rained on during construction.

CDX is the name to know at the yard: C-grade face, D-grade back, exterior glue. In 1/2-inch, roughly 15/32 actual, it is the traditional wall and roof sheathing; in 5/8 and 3/4 inch it decks floors and flat roofs. For subfloors, the purpose-made product is a tongue-and-groove panel, commonly 23/32 or 7/8 inch, whose milled edges interlock between joists so that a footstep at a panel edge cannot deflect one sheet independently of its neighbor and crack the tile or squeak the floor above. Good practice glues the subfloor to the joists with construction adhesive and fastens with ring-shank nails or screws, which is what the squeak-free floor of a well-built house is made of. Underlayment is a different, thinner product, a smooth plugged-face panel laid over the structural subfloor to give vinyl or tile a flawless base; its face grade matters because every dent telegraphs through resilient flooring.

Installation rules exist because panels move and structures flex, and they are printed on the stamp and the builder codes for a reason. Panels go down with the face grain, the long dimension, perpendicular to the framing, which uses the panel's strong axis to span between supports; the span rating assumes this orientation. End joints land on framing and are staggered from row to row like running-bond brickwork so no single joist line carries a continuous seam. A 1/8-inch gap is left at panel edges and ends, about the thickness of a carpenter's pencil, because a rained-on panel field with no gaps will buckle into ridges when it swells. Nail schedules, typically every 6 inches along panel edges and every 12 inches in the field with 8d nails for sheathing, are what make the shear wall calculation true; missing the framing with a row of nails, or overdriving them through the face veneer with an aggressive nail gun, genuinely weakens the wall.

Buyers should understand the relationship with OSB, treated fully in its own section: for most sheathing and subfloor duties the two are code-equivalent when carrying the same span rating, OSB is cheaper, and plywood's remaining advantages are lower weight for the same rating, better fastener performance near edges, faster drying after a soaking, and less edge swelling. Where budgets allow, many builders still specify plywood for roofs, which see the worst wetting and the hottest temperatures, and for floors that will take hardwood or tile. For outdoor projects around the home, remember what X does and does not promise: CDX survives weather during construction, but a doghouse, gate or planter that lives outside permanently wants a true Exterior-rated panel, proper edge sealing and a paint or stain film, or better still, a naturally durable solid wood.

sections.heading: Cabinet-Grade Hardwood Plywood and Core Choices
sections.body:
Hardwood plywood is the panel of furniture and cabinetry: a decorative face veneer, birch, maple, oak, cherry, walnut and beyond, bonded to an engineered core, sold in the same 4 by 8 sheets as construction panels but built for appearance, flatness and machinability rather than span ratings. Understanding it means separating the two questions a sales sheet answers: what is the face, and what is the core. The face question is one of species, cut and grade, covered under grading; the core question deserves its own treatment because it determines the panel's weight, flatness, screw-holding, edge quality and price, and because the same maple face can be had on four very different cores.

Veneer core is traditional plywood construction all the way through: alternating hardwood or softwood veneers, commonly poplar, aspen or fir, under the show faces. It is the lightest of the cores, roughly 70 pounds for a 3/4-inch sheet, the strongest and stiffest, and by far the best at holding screws, which makes it the default for cabinet boxes that hang on walls and for anything assembled with fasteners. Its weaknesses are flatness and edges: veneer core panels can arrive with gentle bow and can have small internal voids that appear as gaps when you cut the sheet, ugly under a routed edge and troublesome for exposed-edge designs. Import quality varies widely; the best domestic and Baltic panels have more, thinner, more uniform plies.

MDF core puts the same face veneers over a slab of medium-density fiberboard. It is the flattest and most uniform option, with a dead-smooth substrate that telegraphs nothing through thin face veneers, and its edges machine cleanly with no voids, which is why shops choose it for veneered doors, panels that must stay flat, and work that will be seen edge-on with banding. The costs are weight, an MDF-core sheet runs 15 to 25 pounds heavier than its veneer-core twin, and mediocre screw-holding, especially into edges. Particleboard core is the budget version of the same idea, common under melamine and plastic laminate in commercial casework: flat, cheap, stable, heavy, and the weakest at fasteners and in moisture. Lumber core, strips of solid wood, often basswood or poplar, edge-glued and sandwiched between crossbands and faces, is the premium old-fashioned construction, excellent for long shelves because of its stiffness and for edges that will be shaped, but it is now a special-order rarity in North America. Combination or combi-core, veneer plies with MDF crossbands directly under the faces, splits the difference deliberately: near-veneer-core weight and screw-holding with near-MDF-core surface smoothness, and it has become the standard offering at many suppliers.

Choosing among cores is a matter of ranking your needs. Wall cabinets and anything screwed together favor veneer core. Full-overlay veneered doors and tabletops favor MDF core or combi. Painted work is usually better served by MDF itself than by paint-grade birch plywood, whose grain and patches telegraph through paint. Shelving asks for stiffness: a 3/4-inch veneer-core shelf on 32-inch spans sags visibly under books over time, so plan on 30 inches or less, thicker panels, or a glued-on solid edge that acts as a stiffening rib. Finally, buy all the panels for one project at one time from one source; cores, thicknesses, and face color shift between mills and batches, and a cabinet run mixing them will fight you at every joint, since actual thickness commonly runs a hair under nominal and varies by core type.

sections.heading: Baltic Birch and Void-Free Plywoods
sections.body:
Baltic birch is the plywood woodworkers praise by name. Made traditionally in Russia, Finland and the Baltic states, it is birch throughout: many thin, uniform birch veneers, each about 1.4 millimeters, laid up with no interior voids, so an 18-millimeter panel, roughly 3/4 inch, carries thirteen plies where a domestic cabinet panel of the same thickness might have seven including two paper-thin faces. The classic sheet size is 1525 by 1525 millimeters, the 5 by 5 foot square that surprises first-time buyers, though 4 by 8 and 5 by 10 sheets are milled for export. Grading runs B for a clean single-piece face, BB allowing small football-shaped patches, then CP and C for shop grades; both faces are graded, a B/BB sheet being the common furniture choice.

The construction pays off in specific ways. The dense, void-free edge machines crisply and, sanded and oiled or clear-coated, is handsome enough that exposed plywood edges became a deliberate design language, in drawer sides, jigs, skateboard ramps, laser-cut goods and modernist furniture. Screw-holding is excellent in both face and edge because there is real birch everywhere a thread lands. Stiffness and strength are outstanding for the thickness, and the panel tolerates routing, finger-jointing and dovetailing that would shred a void-ridden core. For shop fixtures, router jigs and anything that must hold its shape while being dragged around, it has no equal at its price. Drawer boxes from 12-millimeter Baltic birch with a bottom in 6-millimeter are close to a standard recipe in custom shops.

It is not perfect. Faces are rotary-cut and bland compared with sliced hardwood veneers, and they can be thin enough that aggressive sanding burns through; the patches in BB faces show through clear finishes; sheets can arrive with bow, and quality varies by mill; birch's fine, blotchy-staining surface makes it a poor candidate for dark stains without a conditioner or toner. Since 2022, trade sanctions on Russian birch plywood have scrambled the market, raising prices and bringing in substitutes of varying honesty, so the name on the unit matters more than it used to; European mills, and lookalikes from elsewhere, fill the racks with products from excellent to disappointing.

Baltic birch sits inside a wider family of void-free, multi-ply panels worth knowing. ApplePly is the well-known North American equivalent, alder and birch in the same many-thin-plies construction, in 4 by 8 sheets. Aircraft plywood, historically ordered to specifications such as MIL-P-6070, uses birch or mahogany faces over poplar cores in thin metric sizes down to fractions of a millimeter, with fully waterproof glue, sold for model-making and experimental aircraft. Marine plywood, treated with the moisture ratings later in this guide, shares the void-free requirement for a different reason, trapped water. At the opposite end, thin bending plywoods, sold as wacky wood or bendy ply, put all their plies in one direction so the panel rolls into columns and curved aprons. The unifying lesson of the family is that ply count and void discipline, more than face species, are what you feel in the second hundred cuts: uniform cores cut, screw and wear predictably, and predictability is what a maker is actually buying.

sections.heading: MDF: Medium-Density Fiberboard Up Close
sections.body:
Medium-density fiberboard is wood rebuilt from its individual fibers. Mill residues and pulp chips are steamed and fed through a refiner, which grinds them between plates into a fluff of separated cellulose fibers; the fibers are blended with about 8 to 10 percent resin, traditionally urea-formaldehyde, plus a little wax for water resistance, formed into a thick mat, and hot-pressed into panels with a density of roughly 600 to 800 kilograms per cubic meter, around 45 to 50 pounds per cubic foot. Commercialized in the United States in the mid-1960s, MDF answered a specific need: a panel with no grain, no knots, no voids and no layers, uniform enough to machine a molding profile straight into its face. That uniformity remains the whole point. A sheet of MDF is the same material everywhere, in every direction, which no tree ever grew.

Its virtues follow directly. MDF is the flattest common panel and among the most dimensionally stable in changing humidity. Its faces are glass-smooth and take paint better than any veneer; its edges, unlike plywood's striped and voided edge, machine into crisp profiles with router bits and shaper cutters, which is why painted cabinet doors, applied moldings, radius work and templates are MDF territory. It is inexpensive, consistent sheet to sheet, and free of the internal stresses that make solid wood and even plywood move when ripped. Speaker builders prize its acoustic deadness; pattern and jig makers prize the fact that a shape cut today matches one cut next year.

The vices are equally definite. Weight first: a 3/4-inch 4 by 8 sheet runs about 95 pounds, punishing to carry and hard on hinges and hardware. Screw-holding is mediocre in the face and poor in the edge, and driving a screw into an edge without a pilot hole reliably splits the panel; the fix is pilot holes sized to the screw's root, straight-shank screws such as confirmats or deep-thread cabinet screws, and never countersinking aggressively, or better, joinery that does not rely on edge screws at all. Water is the enemy: a soaked edge swells thickly and permanently, so raw MDF has no business near sinks, floors or exteriors unless it is the green-tinted moisture-resistant grade, and even that is for damp air, not standing water. Sag is real; MDF shelves need shorter spans or stiffening edges compared with plywood. And it is hungry for finish at the edges, which drink paint; the cure is to seal edges with glue size, shellac-based primer or a solvent primer, sand, and then topcoat.

Dust and formaldehyde deserve their own paragraph. Machining MDF produces clouds of very fine dust that hangs in the air, and the classic resin releases formaldehyde gas, which the IARC classifies as carcinogenic to humans; modern panels sold in North America must meet CARB Phase 2 and TSCA Title VI emission limits, and NAF and ULEF panels use cleaner chemistry, but the dust itself remains an irritant regardless of resin. Cut MDF with dust extraction at the tool, ventilate, and wear a fitted respirator. Variants complete the picture: hardboard-smooth premium grades for painting, moisture-resistant green, fire-rated pink or red, lightweight grades for theater sets, deep-machinable grades for carved doors, and HDF, a denser thinner cousin used for door skins and laminate-flooring cores. Used where flatness, machinability and paint matter, and kept dry and well supported, MDF is not a cheap substitute for wood; it is the correct engineering answer to a different question.

sections.heading: Particleboard and Melamine Panels
sections.body:
Particleboard is the least glamorous panel in the rack and one of the most used. Where MDF starts from refined fibers, particleboard starts from particles, sawdust, shavings and chipped mill residue, graded by size, blended with urea-formaldehyde resin, and pressed in layers: finer particles are concentrated at the two faces for smoothness, coarser ones in the core for bulk, which is why a cut edge shows a gradient like a geological section. Densities overlap MDF's but typical furniture-grade board is a little lighter and a lot cheaper, and cheapness with flatness is exactly its job: particleboard is the invisible substrate under most plastic-laminate countertops, the carcass material of most flat-pack and commercial cabinetry, and the core of most melamine shelving.

Its working properties set the rules. Faces are smooth but the core is comparatively weak and crumbly, so plain screws hold indifferently and edge screws hold poorly; the flat-pack industry solved this with purpose-made fasteners, coarse-thread euro screws, confirmat screws that thread into a drilled pilot like a machine screw, and the cam-and-dowel fittings familiar from every bookshelf carton, all engineered to grip particle cores. Sharp carbide tooling cuts it cleanly, though it dulls edges faster than solid wood; routed profiles are not worth attempting, since the core tears rather than slices, another reason its edges are always banded or capped. Water ruins it faster than any other panel: a wet edge swells, blisters the laminate above it, and never comes back, which is why a failed dishwasher announces itself as a bulging countertop seam. Moisture-resistant grades exist and are worth specifying for kitchen and bath casework, but the real protection is design that keeps edges sealed and water directed elsewhere.

Melamine board deserves its own explanation because so many projects start as a stack of it. The panel is particleboard, or sometimes MDF, faced at the factory with paper sheets saturated in melamine resin and fused under heat and pressure, a product formally called thermally fused laminate, TFL. The result is a hard, cleanable, pre-finished surface in white, colors and convincing woodgrain prints, at a fraction of the cost of veneered and finished plywood, and it is the default interior of modern cabinets. Its two famous frustrations both have cures. First, the brittle face chips at the cut line; the fixes are a sharp high-tooth-count blade designed for laminates, a zero-clearance throat plate, a scoring cut, a light pass a millimeter deep before the through cut, or a track saw or panel saw with a scoring blade, plus painter's tape on the cut line in a pinch. Second, ordinary wood glue does not bond the melamine face, so joints must be cut through to the core, dadoes and rabbets, or made with fasteners; iron-on melamine edge banding covers the raw edges.

Buying advice is short. Use particleboard and melamine where they excel, dry interior casework, closet systems, shop cabinets, laminate substrates, and budget shelving with supports every 24 inches or so, and refuse them where they fail, wet locations, structural spans, and anywhere fasteners must be removed and redriven repeatedly. Check sheets for flatness, since thin melamine stock can arrive bowed; store them dead flat; and respect the weight, a 3/4-inch melamine sheet is as punishing as MDF. Treated as a system with its own fasteners and edge treatments rather than as ersatz plywood, particleboard is honest, predictable and, per cabinet, very hard to beat on cost.

sections.heading: OSB: Oriented Strand Board
sections.body:
Oriented strand board is the panel that sheathes most new North American houses, and it is a triumph of getting structural performance out of cheap fiber. It is made from strands, thin rectangular flakes of wood a few inches long, cut from small, fast-growing logs, aspen, poplar and southern pine chief among them. The strands are dried, coated with a small percentage of waterproof resin, phenol-formaldehyde or polymeric MDI, plus wax, and formed into a mat in three to five layers, with the strands in the face layers oriented roughly along the panel's length and the core layers cross-oriented or random. Hot pressing fuses the mat into a panel that mimics plywood's cross-banded logic with strands instead of veneers. Waferboard, its unoriented ancestor from the 1960s, lacked the directional strength; orienting the strands, commercialized in the early 1980s, is what made the product structural, and by the turn of the century OSB had passed plywood in sheathing market share on price alone.

Rated OSB carries the same APA-style stamps as plywood, the same span ratings, the same Exposure 1 glue classification, and for shear walls, roofs and subfloors the codes treat equal ratings as equal. Its real differences are practical. OSB is heavier than plywood at the same thickness and rating. It is more uniform, no voids, no knots, and its large sheets, available in lengths up to 12 feet and beyond, suit tall walls. It holds nails driven through its field about as well as plywood but is weaker at panel edges, where strands can pull free. Its signature weakness is water at the edges: a soaked OSB edge wicks moisture into the strand ends and swells into a permanent ridge, which telegraphs through shingles and finish floors, and it dries out far more slowly than plywood after a wetting. Builders answer with factory edge seals, on good subfloor products, rain-screen details, and scheduling that gets roofs dried in promptly. Premium subfloor versions, sold under names like AdvanTech, use denser mats and more resin to earn long warranties against edge swell, and integrated-membrane wall systems such as ZIP sheathing laminate a weather barrier onto the panel at the factory.

Working OSB is straightforward: ordinary carbide blades cut it, though the resin content dulls steel quickly; it drills and nails without splitting; screws hold acceptably in the field. It is not a finish material, its surface is a pebbled collage that no sanding will make furniture-smooth, though that same texture has a fashion following in exposed lofts and shop interiors, usually under several coats of clear finish. For shelving and cabinetry it is the wrong panel; for wall, roof and floor structure, temporary protection, shop fixtures, packing cases and the backs of things, it is the cheapest rated strength you can buy.

One cousin deserves mention because the distinction matters at the yard. LSL, laminated strand lumber, and OSL are strand products pressed into thick billets and sawn into studs, rim boards and headers, structural lumber from the same fiber logic. And one caution: OSB's Exposure 1 rating, like plywood's, covers construction-phase weather, not service exposure; an OSB shed floor or doghouse left to the rain will swell, delaminate at the edges and grow mushrooms with impressive speed. Keep it structural, keep it dry, detail its edges, and OSB will quietly do the most load-bearing work per dollar of anything in this guide.

sections.heading: Hardboard, Pegboard and Specialty Panels
sections.body:
Hardboard is the thin, dense, brown panel everyone has handled, the back of the bookcase, the bottom of the drawer, the clipboard under the paper. It is a fiber panel like MDF but denser, made by pressing wood fibers at high temperature until the wood's own lignin, sometimes helped by a little added resin, bonds them into a hard sheet, typically 1/8 to 1/4 inch thick, around 60 pounds per cubic foot. The classic wet process gives one smooth face and one screened, waffle-textured back, S1S; dry-process board is smooth both sides, S2S. The material's proprietary history is written on its common name: Masonite, after William H. Mason, who developed the wet process in Laurel, Mississippi in 1924, when a stuck press valve accidentally produced a dense, coherent board from exploded wood fiber. Tempered hardboard is the upgraded version, treated with oil or extra resin and heat-cured for greater hardness, stiffness and moisture resistance; it is the one to buy for anything that flexes or gets handled.

Hardboard's jobs are the thin-panel jobs. Cabinet backs and drawer bottoms captured in grooves, where its stability and low cost are perfect. Dust panels, templates and patterns, tempered hardboard routs cleanly and wears well against a bearing, and a template made from it costs pennies. Protective surfaces: painters and floor refinishers sheet whole rooms in it, and a hardboard skin on a workbench top takes the abuse and is replaced for a few dollars. Door skins on hollow-core doors, the substrate of chalkboards, economy paneling, and, with a baked enamel face, dry-erase boards. It bends to gentle curves, which furniture and display makers exploit. Its limits mirror MDF's, concentrated: it hates water, it holds screws barely at all, so it is captured, glued, stapled or nailed rather than screwed, and it is a panel for skins and backs, not structure.

Pegboard is hardboard's most famous form, perforated with 1/8- or 1/4-inch holes on a 1-inch grid to accept wire hooks; the shop-organization systems of the twentieth century were built on it, and the rule of hanging it on furring strips so hooks can pass behind still applies. Beyond hardboard, the specialty rack holds several panels a maker should recognize. Bending plywood, all plies running one way, wraps columns and curved cabinet aprons. Doorskin plywood, 1/8-inch mahogany-faced, is the model-maker's and template-maker's friend. Prefinished plywood, birch or maple with a factory UV-cured coat on one or both faces, saves the worst finishing job in cabinetmaking, the insides of boxes, and is worth its premium in any kitchen build. Marine plywood and MDO await the moisture section; MDO, medium-density overlay, is exterior plywood faced with a resin-soaked paper, the traditional signboard and concrete-form panel, and the best-painting exterior panel there is; its sibling HDO carries a harder overlay for form work. Cement board, magnesium-oxide board and gypsum panels are the mineral cousins that take over where water and fire rule out wood entirely.

The practical habit this section should leave you with is thinking in skins and cores. Much of woodworking's economy lies in putting a cheap, stable panel where nobody looks, a hardboard back squaring a cabinet, a doorskin template guiding a router, a prefinished interior saving a weekend, and spending money and figure only on the faces the eye and hand actually meet.

sections.heading: Glues, Moisture Ratings and Marine Plywood
sections.body:
What separates an interior panel from an exterior one is mostly chemistry, and the chemistry is worth understanding because water is how sheet goods die. Urea-formaldehyde, the traditional interior resin of hardwood plywood, particleboard and MDF, is strong, cheap and colorless, but it hydrolyzes: sustained moisture breaks the glue itself, and the panel delaminates or crumbles regardless of how sound its wood is. Phenol-formaldehyde, the dark glue line of construction plywood and OSB, is essentially waterproof once cured; boiling does not undo it, which is why old specifications called such glue lines WBP, weather and boil proof. Melamine-urea blends sit between, moisture-resistant rather than waterproof. Polymeric MDI, used in much OSB and in NAF fiber panels, is likewise highly water-resistant and adds no formaldehyde. The critical insight is that glue and wood are separate questions: CDX has waterproof glue wrapped around knotty, gap-prone veneers, so the panel survives wetting as a structure while its surface checks and its voids trap water. Exterior performance requires both waterproof glue and veneers good enough not to trap or admit water, which is exactly the definition of the marine grades.

The rating ladder, in the American vocabulary: Interior panels, UF glue, must stay dry, period. Exposure 1, waterproof glue with interior-grade veneers, tolerates construction-phase weather and occasional wetting but not service exposure; most sheathing OSB and much CDX is Exposure 1. Exterior, waterproof glue with C-grade or better veneers throughout, is rated for permanent weather exposure, fences, soffits, outdoor furniture substrates, and includes finish-oriented products like MDO. Marine grade sits at the top: the same waterproof phenolic glue, but with A or B faces, higher-grade inner plies, and crucially no voids, so there are no hidden pockets to hold water and start rot, and no weak spots when the panel is bent over a boat frame. The common imported standard is BS 1088, British Standard marine plywood, typically in okoume, meranti or sapele; okoume is light and fair but not itself rot-resistant, a point that surprises people. Marine plywood is not pressure-treated and is not rot-proof; it is void-free, well-glued plywood that, in boat practice, is always sealed, traditionally with epoxy coatings and fiberglass cloth, and its price reflects veneer quality, not magic.

Practical moisture rules follow. First, edges are everything: end grain and core edges drink water tens of times faster than faces, so seal cut edges of any outdoor panel with epoxy, exterior primer or at minimum several flooded coats of paint, and design so edges do not sit in puddles, gap decking, drip edges, feet under posts. Second, finish both faces alike to keep the panel balanced, and remember that dark paint in the sun cooks glue lines and drives moisture cycling. Third, pressure-treated plywood exists for ground-adjacent and high-rot situations, sill sheathing, planter boxes, trailer decks, and combines exterior glue with preservative-infused veneers; use fasteners rated for the treatment chemicals, since modern copper-based treatments corrode plain steel. Fourth, for wet rooms indoors, tile substrates belong to cement board and membrane systems, not to any wood panel, however rated. And for the perennial question, can I use this leftover panel outside, the honest test is to read the stamp for the glue class, look at the edge for voids, and then assume the answer is no unless you are prepared to seal every edge and repaint on schedule; weather is patient, and it always finds the shortcut you left it.

sections.heading: Choosing the Right Panel for the Job
sections.body:
Panel choice becomes easy when you interrogate the job instead of the shelf. Six questions do the work. Will it live dry or wet? Anything outdoors, in a garage that sweats, or near plumbing pushes you toward exterior-glued plywood, sealed edges and paint, and away from MDF and particleboard entirely. Does it carry load? Structure wants rated plywood or OSB at the stamped span; shelves want stiffness, which means plywood or lumber-core with solid edging, generous thickness, or short spans. Will it be painted, clear-finished or laminated? Paint loves MDF; clear finish loves good veneer faces or Baltic birch edges; laminate and melamine want particleboard or MDF substrates. Will fasteners be driven, and re-driven? Screws favor veneer-core plywood; knock-down hardware tolerates particle cores; nothing loves screws into MDF edges. How flat must it stay, and how flat must it start? Doors and tabletops argue for MDF-core or combi-core; jigs argue for Baltic birch or tempered hardboard. And what does failure cost? A sagging closet shelf is an annoyance; a failed van floor or a delaminated boat transom is a different category, and the panel budget should reflect it.

Run the common projects through those questions and the standard answers appear. Kitchen and built-in cabinets: 3/4-inch veneer-core plywood boxes, prefinished if you can get it, 1/2-inch backs, MDF or MDF-core for painted doors and any large flat slab, drawer boxes in 1/2-inch Baltic birch, melamine acceptable for closets and garage cabinets on a budget. Bookshelves: 3/4-inch plywood with a glued 1-1/2-inch solid wood front edge, spans held to about 30 to 32 inches for book loads, or thicker panels if the design demands longer runs. Workshop: OSB or CDX for utility surfaces and French-cleat walls, tempered hardboard as a sacrificial bench skin, Baltic birch for jigs, fences and router templates. Painted trim, radius work and interior moldings: MDF where dry, primed all around. Outdoor projects: exterior plywood or MDO for painted work, marine grades plus epoxy for boats and anything flexing in the weather, pressure-treated panels near ground, and honest solid cedar or the composites where standing water is the design condition. Speaker boxes and machine bases: MDF for deadness. Van and trailer floors: void-free structural plywood, sealed everywhere.

Budget strategy matters as much as selection. Prices step steeply with face grade, so put A faces only where eyes land, and use shop-grade or C2 sheets for hidden parts; many yards sell blemished shop sheets at deep discounts that are perfect for interiors and jigs. Mind actual thickness: nominal 3/4 panels run 23/32 or 18 millimeters depending on origin, and undersized-plywood router bits and dado stacks exist precisely because of it; measure the actual sheets before cutting joinery. Check every sheet at purchase, sight the length for bow and twist, inspect edges for voids and core gaps, and reject water stains, because no discount repays fighting a banana through a table saw. Buy the whole project from one batch, haul sheets flat or fully supported on a rack, and if the yard offers a panel saw, have them break sheets down to rough oversize pieces; two straight cuts at the store turn an unmanageable 95-pound slab into parts one person can mill safely at home, and the cut is usually free.

sections.heading: Cutting Sheet Goods Cleanly and Safely
sections.body:
Cutting a full sheet well is a problem of support, tooling and tear-out, in that order. Support first: a 4 by 8 panel must be held so it cannot sag into the blade, pinch the kerf or fall as the cut completes. The simple universal answer is a sacrificial foam bed, a sheet of 1-1/2- or 2-inch rigid insulation on the floor or across sawhorses; lay the panel on it, set the blade to protrude only about 1/4 inch below the panel, and the offcut never falls, the panel never pinches, and the saw cannot reach anything that matters. Pinching is the mechanism of kickback, the saw or panel being hurled when the kerf closes on the blade, which is why open-frame sawhorse cuts on an unsupported middle are how sheet-cutting accidents happen. On the table saw, a full sheet is only safe with infeed and outfeed support and a helper or sliding table; the better workflow in a small shop is to break the sheet down with a circular saw first and bring only manageable pieces to the table saw for final sizing.

Tooling second. Tear-out, the splintering of the face veneer or melamine at the cut, happens where teeth exit the material. A circular saw's teeth cut upward, so its tear-out lands on the top face: cut sheet goods good face down with a circular saw. A table saw's teeth enter from the top: feed good face up. Blade choice is the single biggest lever: a sharp 40-tooth general blade serves plywood adequately; a 60- to 80-tooth high-ATB or triple-chip blade is the answer for melamine, laminates and veneer faces; and a dull blade of any count both burns and chips. A zero-clearance insert on the table saw backs up the veneer at the exit; painter's tape on the cut line, a scored line from a utility knife against a straightedge, or a 1-millimeter-deep scoring pass before the through cut each buy a cleaner second face when the setup cannot. A track saw, a plunge circular saw riding an aluminum guide rail with an anti-chip strip, is the modern solution to the whole problem, delivering table-saw-quality edges on full sheets on the foam bed; a shop-made guide, a straightedge screwed to a hardboard base trimmed by the saw itself, does most of the same job for the cost of scraps.

Dust and personal protection are not optional extras with sheet goods. MDF and particleboard cutting fills air with fine dust and formaldehyde-bearing particles; connect the saw to extraction where possible, cut outside when practical, and wear a fitted N95 or P100 respirator, safety glasses and hearing protection for every powered cut. Keep helpers and children out of the plane of the blade, unplug saws to change blades, and let the blade stop before lifting any saw out of a cut.
steps: Plan the cut list on paper first, drawing each sheet and arranging parts so factory edges land where straightness matters and the good face is oriented for the saw you will use.
Lay rigid foam insulation on a flat floor or across low sawhorses and place the sheet on it, good face down for a circular or track saw.
Set blade depth so the teeth protrude no more than about 1/4 inch below the panel.
Mark the cut, then clamp a guide rail or straightedge offset for your saw's base, checking the offset with a test scrap.
Put on respirator, safety glasses and hearing protection, and connect dust extraction if available.
Score the cut line through the face veneer with a utility knife, or apply painter's tape over it, when the show face must be flawless.
Stand to one side of the cut line, start the saw at full speed before contact, and feed steadily without forcing, letting the blade do the work.
Support long offcuts as the cut completes rather than letting them lever and snap the last inches of veneer.
Move rough parts to the table saw or track saw for final sizing to exact dimensions, feeding good face up on the table saw against a properly set fence.
Vacuum dust from the work, the tools and yourself before leaving the shop, and change out of dusty clothes rather than shaking them indoors.

sections.heading: Edge Treatments: Banding and Solid-Wood Edging
sections.body:
Every panel has four edges that betray what it is, and edge treatment is where sheet-goods work rises or falls. The choices form a ladder of effort. The quickest rung is iron-on edge banding: a roll of real wood veneer, or PVC or melamine to match a laminate face, pre-coated with hot-melt adhesive, sold in widths slightly over the common panel thicknesses. You press it on with a household iron set to medium-hot, moving slowly enough to remelt the glue, rub it down hard with a block while warm, then trim the overhang with a double-edged banding trimmer or a fine file and finish-sand the arrises. Done attentively it is fast, cheap and looks factory-made; its weaknesses are durability at outside corners and kitchens' wet zones, where heat and moisture can lift it, and a tendency to telegraph a hard line under stain. Commercial shops apply the same idea with edgebanders and thicker PVC in 1- to 3-millimeter gauges, whose radiused corners survive real abuse, which is why commercial casework edges look softly rounded.

The sturdier rung is solid wood edging, glued strips of matching or contrasting lumber. A 1/4-by-3/4 strip glued to a shelf edge hides the plies and takes the knocks; a 1-1/2-inch-deep strip glued on edge transforms the same shelf structurally, roughly doubling its stiffness by acting as a beam flange, which is why bookshelf fronts and counter edges wear deep solid noses. Attach with glue alone and clamps, or glue plus brads, blue tape works as a clamp for light strips, then flush-trim with a router bearing bit or a sharp block plane, staying alert to the thin face veneer, which an aggressive pass will cut through in one stroke. Refinements include a slight V-groove where band meets face to make the joint line deliberate, tongue-and-groove or spline alignment for long runs, and profiling the solid edge, roundover, chamfer, bullnose, which pure banding cannot support.

Some designs skip concealment and celebrate the edge. Baltic birch and ApplePly edges, sanded through the grits and clear-finished, read as fine striping and have become a modernist signature; a roundover on a void-free edge looks intentional, while the same treatment on voided construction plywood exposes gaps, which is the whole difference. MDF edges, machined into profiles, need only sealing, glue size, shellac or a specialty edge sealer, then primer, to paint as crisply as the face. Melamine interiors typically get matching pre-glued melamine banding on visible front edges and nothing where a face frame or wall hides them.

Match the treatment to the exposure. Drawer boxes and shop fixtures: eased and sanded raw edges or nothing. Painted built-ins: MDF profiles or paint-grade solid edging, caulked and primed. Stain-grade casework: veneer banding on carcass edges, solid lumber on doors, shelves and everywhere hands land. Counters and desks: solid wood or applied laminate self-edge, never bare banding at a knee line. And in every case, band or edge after cutting to final size but before assembly where possible, because pressing an iron into an assembled cabinet's back corner is a lesson learned once. Kept honest with a sharp trimmer and a sanding block, edging is the highest-return half hour in panel work: it is the difference between a project that reads as plywood and one that reads as furniture.

sections.heading: Fastening, Joinery, Finishing and Flat Storage
sections.body:
Joinery in sheet goods follows one law: panels are strong in their faces and vulnerable at their edges, so good joints either enlarge the glue area or lock faces together mechanically. The workhorses are the dado, a groove across one panel that houses the end of another, the rabbet, a step along an edge that seats a back or a top, and the groove for captured panels; each turns a weak butt joint into aligned, load-bearing shoulders and is cut quickly with a dado stack, a router, or repeated table-saw passes. Modern fastener systems supplement them: pocket screws pull carcasses together fast in plywood, though they hold indifferently in particle cores; biscuits and dominos align faces; confirmat screws, drilled with their stepped bit, are the correct machine-style fastener for particleboard and MDF; and euro cam-and-dowel hardware makes knockdown furniture possible. Screws into any fiber-panel edge want pilot holes about the root diameter of the screw and straight-shank, deep-thread screws, never tapered woodscrews driven unpiloted, which split MDF as reliably as a wedge. Ordinary PVA wood glue bonds all bare wood-based faces and edges well, though end-grain-like porous MDF edges drink glue and benefit from a sizing coat first; nothing bonds melamine faces, so joints there must reach the core.

Finishing splits by product. Veneer-faced plywood takes stains and clear coats like solid wood with two cautions: the face veneer is thin, so sand with the grain and stop at about 180 grit, over-sanding burns through at corners first, and modern rotary faces can blotch, so test stain on offcuts and consider a conditioner or a toned finish on birch and maple. Edges finish darker than faces; banded or solid edges solve that too. MDF paints beautifully in the field and thirstily at the edges: seal edges, prime everything, sand the primer, then topcoat, spraying if you want a truly slick door. Prefinished plywood removes interior finishing entirely, and a fast shop schedule finishes parts flat, before assembly, masking glue lines, which beats brushing inside a box every time. Whatever the film, coat both faces of unattached panels comparably so moisture exchange stays balanced and the panel stays flat.

Storage and handling close the loop, because sheets are ruined horizontally more often than they are ruined in the cut. The ideal is dead-flat stacking on a level base with stickers aligned vertically; the practical shop compromise is storing sheets on edge, as close to vertical as the rack allows, ideally within about ten degrees of upright and supported along their length, since sheets leaned at a lazy angle for a month take a permanent bow. Keep panels off concrete floors, which wick moisture into the bottom edge, using scrap strips as a curb, and let sheets acclimate in the shop for a few days before precision work. Carry sheets with a panel carrier hook, a rope-and-handle sling, or a second pair of hands, and roll long distances on a dolly; backs are not consumables. A mildly bowed panel can often be tamed by laying it convex side up on damp grass or over damp towels for some hours, dampening the concave face, then stacking it flat under weight to dry, and design can rescue the rest, since a bowed panel screwed into a square carcass with a dado every 16 inches straightens itself. Respect flatness, water and edges, and sheet goods will repay you with furniture, cabinets and structures that stay exactly the shape you built them.

guides.title: Board Foot Measurement and Timber Grading
guides.summary: How lumber is measured, graded, and sold: what a board foot is and how to calculate it, nominal versus actual sizes, the quarter system for hardwood thickness, NHLA hardwood grades and softwood structural grades, reading grade stamps, defects, moisture content, log scaling rules, and how to estimate and buy wood for a project.

sections.heading: What a Board Foot Is and Why Lumber Is Sold by Volume
sections.body:
A board foot is the standard unit of lumber volume in North America, and nearly everything about buying wood makes more sense once you understand it. One board foot is the volume of a board one foot long, one foot wide, and one inch thick: 144 cubic inches of wood. The unit exists because boards come in wildly different shapes. A lumberyard cannot price hardwood by the piece when one walnut board is ten inches wide and six feet long while the next is five inches wide and twelve feet long; pricing by volume puts every board, whatever its proportions, on the same scale. When a dealer quotes cherry at eight dollars a board foot, that number applies equally to wide short boards and narrow long ones, and your bill is simply the total volume you carry out multiplied by the rate.

The abbreviation you will see is BF or bd ft, and in commercial and industrial contexts the unit scales up to MBF, a thousand board feet, which is how sawmills, wholesalers, and commodity markets quote softwood lumber; futures contracts and housing-industry statistics are stated in dollars per thousand board feet. At the other end of the scale, a hobbyist buying a single board is doing the same arithmetic on a smaller number. Firewood, by contrast, is sold by the cord, a stacked volume measure, and pulpwood by weight, because neither use cares about the shape of the pieces; the board foot exists precisely for wood whose value lies in being sawn into usable rectangles.

It matters to understand from the start that the board foot is a nominal volume unit, tied to the dimensions by which lumber is named and tallied rather than always to the wood you can actually measure with calipers. In softwood dimension lumber, a two-by-four is tallied as two inches by four inches even though it actually measures one and a half by three and a half after drying and planing, a system explained in its own section below. In hardwood, thickness is tallied in the rough-sawn dimension, so a board sold as four-quarter, meaning one inch, may reach you planed to thirteen sixteenths yet still be billed at the full inch. None of this is sharp practice; it is a standardized convention that the whole industry shares, but it means the volume on your invoice is the volume before the mill's finishing work, and your project math must account for the difference.

A sense of scale helps make the unit concrete. A typical eight-foot two-by-four contains five and a third board feet. A hardwood board one inch thick, six inches wide, and eight feet long contains four board feet. A modest bookcase might consume twenty to thirty board feet of hardwood; a dining table, sixty to a hundred; a small house's framing package runs into the thousands. North American mills produce tens of billions of board feet of lumber annually, and the same unit runs unbroken from that industrial scale down to the single plank under your arm, which is exactly what a good unit is for.

sections.heading: Calculating Board Feet: The Formula and Worked Examples
sections.body:
The board foot formula is simple enough to do in your head at the lumber rack once you have practiced it. Multiply thickness in inches by width in inches by length in inches, and divide by 144, the number of cubic inches in a board foot. Because lumber lengths are usually known in feet, the everyday version substitutes length in feet and divides by 12 instead: thickness in inches times width in inches times length in feet, divided by 12. Both give identical answers; use whichever fits the numbers in front of you.

Work a few examples until the pattern settles. A board one inch thick, six inches wide, and eight feet long: one times six times eight is 48, divided by 12 is four board feet. A two-by-four that is eight feet long: two times four times eight is 64, divided by 12 is 5.33 board feet, and note that you use the nominal two and four, not the actual inch and a half and three and a half, because the tally system runs on nominal sizes. A plank two inches thick, ten inches wide, and twelve feet long: two times ten times twelve is 240, divided by 12 is twenty board feet. An eight-quarter hardwood board, meaning two inches thick in the rough, that is seven and a quarter inches wide and ten feet long: two times 7.25 times ten is 145, divided by 12 is just over twelve board feet. Hardwood dealers measure the actual width and length of each board, because hardwood comes in random widths and lengths, but they use the rough quarter thickness even if the board has been surfaced thinner.

A few conventions smooth real transactions. Widths are commonly measured to the nearest inch or half inch depending on the yard's practice, and fractional board-foot totals are rounded, usually in the seller's favor at the tally but trivially so on any normal purchase. Thickness below one inch is still tallied as one inch in most hardwood yards, so half-inch resawn stock often bills the same as four-quarter; ask before assuming. For a stack of identical pieces, compute one and multiply: fifteen eight-foot two-by-sixes are two times six times eight divided by 12, which is eight board feet each, 120 board feet for the lift. Going the other way, if a project calls for 45 board feet of four-quarter maple and the yard's boards average six inches wide and eight feet long, each board holds four board feet, so you need a dozen boards before any waste allowance.

Price conversion is the last habit. Multiply total board feet by the per-board-foot rate: 32 board feet of walnut at twelve dollars is 384 dollars. When softwood is priced per thousand board feet, move the decimal: framing lumber at 450 dollars per MBF is 45 cents a board foot, so that 5.33 board-foot stud contains about two dollars and forty cents of wood at the commodity price, with the rest of its retail cost being milling, transport, and margin. The steps below condense the procedure you will actually use standing at the rack.
steps: Read or measure the board's thickness in inches, using the nominal or quarter designation for the tally rather than the planed dimension.
Measure the width in inches at a representative point, and for tapered hardwood boards measure near the middle of the length.
Measure the length in feet, rounding down to the yard's tally increment if you are estimating your bill conservatively.
Multiply thickness by width by length in feet, then divide the result by 12 to get board feet for that piece.
Repeat for each different size in your load, multiply identical pieces by their count, and add the results for the total.
Multiply total board feet by the quoted price per board foot, or divide a per-MBF price by 1000 first, to get the cost of the wood.
Add your project's waste factor, typically 15 to 30 percent, before deciding how much to actually purchase.

sections.heading: Nominal Versus Actual Dimensions in Softwood Lumber
sections.body:
The most notorious fact in the lumberyard is that a two-by-four is not two inches by four inches. It actually measures one and a half by three and a half inches, and every standard dimension size carries a similar reduction. The names are called nominal dimensions, from the Latin for name, and the true measurements are called actual or dressed dimensions. Nothing is being stolen: the nominal size describes the rough green board as it was first sawn from the log, and the actual size is what remains after the board has been dried, which shrinks it, and surfaced smooth on all four sides, which planes away more. The industry standardized the relationship so that every mill's two-by-four finishes to the same actual size, and the American Softwood Lumber Standard, PS 20, maintained under the Department of Commerce, fixes the numbers.

The pattern of reductions is worth memorizing because it is regular. For thicknesses and widths under two inches nominal, subtract a quarter inch: a one-by board is three quarters of an inch thick. For dimensions from two up through six inches nominal, subtract half an inch: a two-by-four is one and a half by three and a half, a two-by-six is one and a half by five and a half, a four-by-four is three and a half square. For nominal widths of eight inches and above, subtract three quarters of an inch: a two-by-eight is one and a half by seven and a quarter, a two-by-ten is one and a half by nine and a quarter, a two-by-twelve is one and a half by eleven and a quarter, and a one-by-twelve is three quarters by eleven and a quarter. Lengths, by contrast, are honest: an eight-foot stud is eight feet, and precut studs for standard walls come in specific lengths like 92 and five eighths inches, designed so that plates plus stud build a standard eight-foot wall.

The history explains the oddity. Early sawmills sold rough lumber at full nominal size, and builders planed it, or did not, themselves. As surfaced lumber became the norm in the early twentieth century, mills planed the rough boards and shipped the smaller result under the old names, and decades of negotiation among mills, builders, and regulators settled the standardized dressed sizes largely in the form finalized in the 1960s revision of the softwood standard. Court cases have occasionally tested whether selling a one and a half inch board as a two-by-four is deceptive, and the settled answer is that the nominal name is a trade designation, lawful so long as the actual dimension standard is met, which is why big-box stores now print both on the shelf tag.

For the builder and maker, the practical consequences are constant. Structural span tables and engineering values are computed on actual dimensions, so no strength is missing from what the tables promise. Layout math must use actual sizes: two two-by-fours face to face are three inches, not four; a four-by-four post is three and a half inches square, which is why the notch you cut from the plans fits. And when replacing old-house framing, measure it, because lumber from before standardization is often a true two inches, and a modern board will sit proud or shy in the old pocket. The one place nominal size still rules is the tally: board feet are computed on nominal dimensions for dimension lumber, which slightly flatters the volume, and the market long ago priced that in.

sections.heading: The Quarter System: 4/4, 5/4, and 8/4 Hardwood Thicknesses
sections.body:
Hardwood lumber speaks its own dialect of thickness, the quarter system, and understanding it marks the difference between a first-time visitor and a customer the yard takes seriously. Thickness is expressed in quarters of an inch as sawn in the rough: four-quarter, written 4/4, is one inch; five-quarter, 5/4, is one and a quarter inches; six-quarter, 6/4, is one and a half; eight-quarter, 8/4, is two inches; twelve-quarter, 12/4, is three inches; and sixteen-quarter, 16/4, is a full four inches. The terms are spoken exactly as written, four-quarter and eight-quarter, and they always refer to the thickness the sawyer cut at the mill, before any drying shrinkage or planing.

The reason hardwood clings to rough measure while softwood standardized dressed sizes lies in how the two are used. Softwood dimension lumber goes into framing, where every stud must match its neighbors, so the mill surfaces everything to identical actual sizes. Hardwood goes to furniture makers, cabinet shops, and instrument builders, who each need different final thicknesses and want to do their own flattening. A woodworker buying 4/4 stock expects to joint one face flat and plane to a final three quarters or seven eighths of an inch; buying the wood already skimmed thin would steal the very material needed to remove cup and twist and to hit a precise dimension. So hardwood is sold rough, or lightly surfaced, and the tally stays in the rough quarter thickness either way.

When a yard does surface hardwood, the industry uses standard designations for how much. S2S means surfaced two sides, faces planed and edges left rough; S4S means surfaced four sides; and skip-planed or hit-or-miss means a light pass that cleans most of each face while leaving low spots rough, enough to reveal grain and color for selection while preserving maximum thickness. Standard practice under the National Hardwood Lumber Association rules planes 4/4 to a heavy thirteen sixteenths S2S, 5/4 to a heavy inch and a sixteenth, and 8/4 to a heavy inch and three quarters; the exact figures vary slightly by agreement, but the principle holds that you are billed on the rough quarter size while carrying home something thinner. This is not a trick; the sawdust was part of the board the mill produced, and the pricing convention is uniform across the trade.

Choosing a quarter size is project planning. Standard furniture parts, tabletops at three quarters to seven eighths, come from 4/4. Thicker tops, stair treads, and heavy shelves come from 5/4 or 6/4. Table legs, workbench tops, turning blanks, and bed posts call for 8/4 and up, and the thick sizes cost disproportionately more per board foot because thick stock must be sawn from better logs and dried far more slowly; drying time grows roughly with the square of thickness, and a kiln charge of 8/4 oak ties up capital for many weeks where 4/4 takes days to a few weeks. Resist the beginner's economy of gluing two thin boards to fake a thick one where the edges will show, and resist equally the waste of planing 8/4 down to make a three-quarter panel that 4/4 would have yielded. Buy the quarter size whose rough dimension comfortably contains your finished part, with a sixteenth to an eighth to spare per face for cleanup.

sections.heading: Hardwood Lumber Grades: FAS, Selects, and the Common Grades
sections.body:
Hardwood grading answers a question every furniture maker asks at the rack: how much clear, usable wood will this board yield? The system is administered by the National Hardwood Lumber Association, the NHLA, founded in 1898 precisely to end the chaos of every mill grading by its own lights, and its rulebook remains the trade's constitution in North America, with strong influence worldwide. The essential insight of NHLA grading is that it does not judge a board's beauty; it estimates, by rule, the percentage of the board that can be cut into clear rectangular pieces of specified minimum sizes. Grade is a yield prediction, nothing more, and once you internalize that, the grades stop being mysterious.

The top grade is FAS, a name descended from the old term Firsts and Seconds. An FAS board must be at least six inches wide and eight feet long, and must yield at least 83 and a third percent clear wood, ten twelfths of its surface, in cuttings of at least four inches by five feet or three inches by seven feet. Both faces must make the grade. Just below sits FAS One Face, written F1F, where the better face meets FAS and the poorer face meets Number 1 Common; and Selects, essentially the same one-good-face standard but allowing boards as narrow as four inches and as short as six feet. Selects and F1F exist because a tabletop or door panel shows one face; paying for two perfect faces is often waste. In practice many yards sell a mixed pile labeled Select and Better.

The workhorse grade is Number 1 Common, which requires boards at least three inches wide and four feet long yielding at least 66 and two thirds percent clear wood, eight twelfths, in cuttings of at least four inches by two feet or three inches by three feet. Number 2A Common drops the yield to fifty percent in cuttings of three inches by two feet; Number 3A falls further still. The Common grades are not inferior wood in any absolute sense; they are the same trees, with more or larger defects distributed through the board, and they are the smart buy whenever your parts are short or narrow. A chair maker cutting two-foot legs and rails can often get nearly the same usable yield from Number 1 Common as from FAS at a fraction of the price, while someone building an eight-foot bookcase with full-length sides genuinely needs the long clear runs only the upper grades guarantee.

Two cautions complete the picture. First, grade is assigned to the board as sawn at the mill, from the poorer face for FAS and from defined rules for each grade, and it travels with the lumber through the trade; but retail yards frequently sort, trim, and re-market, so the pile labeled cabinet grade at a small yard may be an informal blend. Ask what NHLA grade a pile was bought as. Second, grading ignores what many buyers care most about: color, figure, and grain match are not grade factors, with narrow exceptions in species like walnut where trade practice adapts, so a plain, perfectly clear board and a spectacular curly one can share a grade. The grade tells you how much clear wood is there; your eye must still choose which clear wood you want.

sections.heading: Clear Cuttings, Surface Measure, and How NHLA Grading Actually Works
sections.body:
Watching a hardwood grader work a board in a few seconds looks like magic, but the procedure underneath is mechanical, and knowing it lets you predict grades yourself. The system rests on three quantities: surface measure, clear cuttings, and cutting units. Surface measure, abbreviated SM, is the area of one face of the board in square feet, found by multiplying width in inches by length in feet and dividing by twelve, rounding to the nearest whole number. A board eight inches wide and twelve feet long has a surface measure of eight. Surface measure deliberately ignores thickness; grade is about the face, and the board-foot tally handles volume separately.

A clear cutting is an imaginary rectangle, free of the defects the rules count, that could be sawn from the board. Each grade defines its minimum cutting sizes and its yield fraction, expressed in twelfths of the surface. FAS demands ten twelfths, 83 and a third percent, in cuttings no smaller than four inches by five feet or three inches by seven feet, and limits how many separate cuttings may be used, generally the surface measure divided by four; Number 1 Common demands eight twelfths, two thirds, in cuttings down to four inches by two feet or three inches by three feet, allowing more of them; Number 2A demands six twelfths, half, in cuttings down to three inches by two feet. The arithmetic runs in cutting units, where one unit is one inch of width by one foot of length: a cutting four inches wide and five feet long contains twenty units. Multiply the board's surface measure by the grade's twelfth-fraction numerator to get required units: an SM 8 board needs 80 units of clear cuttings for FAS, ten times eight, and about 66 for Number 1 Common, eight times eight rounding by rule.

The grader therefore works like this: measure width and length, compute surface measure; inspect the poorer face, since FAS is graded from the poor face and the Commons from the poor face with specified exceptions; mentally lay the largest permissible clear rectangles between the knots, checks, and wane; total the units; and assign the highest grade whose yield, cutting sizes, and cutting count the board satisfies. Experienced graders do this at a glance, hundreds of boards an hour, with chalk in hand, and NHLA runs a residential school in Memphis that still trains graders in exactly this discipline.

The practical power for a buyer is that you can run the same procedure informally at the rack. Faced with a nine-dollar FAS pile and a five-dollar Number 1 Common pile, sketch your actual parts list as rectangles, then eye the common boards and ask whether your rectangles fit between the defects. If your largest part is a 30-inch drawer front, the answer is usually yes, and the savings are large; if you need clear eight-foot runs, it is usually no. Remember too that the rules count defects, not ugliness: sound color variation, mineral streak in maple, and sapwood are not grade defects unless the sale specifies otherwise, so a board can be FAS and still be the wrong wood for your tabletop. Grade math tells you the yield; only you know which cuttings your project actually needs, and the buyer who brings a cutting list to the yard is using the graders' own logic in reverse.

sections.heading: Softwood Grading: Structural Grades and Appearance Grades
sections.body:
Softwood lumber lives a double life, structural and decorative, and it carries two grading systems to match. Structural grading answers an engineering question: how much load can this piece carry? Because wood is a natural material full of knots and sloped grain, every piece of framing lumber in North America is graded, almost all of it visually, by trained graders at the mill working under the supervision of agencies accredited through the American Lumber Standard Committee, the body that also maintains the softwood sizes. The regional agencies you will meet on stamps include the Western Wood Products Association and the West Coast Lumber Inspection Bureau in the West, and the Southern Pine Inspection Bureau in the South, each publishing rulebooks tuned to their species but coordinated so that a Number 2 means comparable things everywhere.

The structural ladder for dimension lumber runs, from the top: Select Structural, then Number 1, Number 2, and Number 3, with companion categories Stud, a grade optimized for vertical members, and the light-framing set Construction, Standard, and Utility for plates and blocking. Grade is assigned by measuring the size and location of knots, the slope of grain relative to the edge, the extent of wane, splits, and other defects, against tables that engineers have converted into published design values: allowable bending stress, stiffness, tension, and compression numbers for each species group and grade, which is what span tables are built from. Number 2 is the everyday framing grade that codes assume for joists and rafters; Select Structural commands a premium for engineered situations; Number 3 and Utility handle blocking and non-structural work. A separate stream, machine stress rated or MSR lumber, is graded by running each piece through a machine that flexes it and measures stiffness directly, yielding tighter, certified values, and MSR stock feeds truss plants and engineered applications where consistency pays.

Appearance grading answers a different question: how good does it look? Boards destined for trim, siding, paneling, and shelving are graded on the quality of their faces, not their strength. In Western species the traditional select ladder runs B and Better, C Select, D Select downward, with knotty grades numbered Common 1 through 5 for boards where tight knots are part of the look; Idaho white pine historically used names like Supreme and Choice. Southern pine uses its own appearance ladder. The practical division at a lumberyard is simpler than the rulebooks: clear grades for paint-and-stain trim at several times the price, and knotty common grades for utility and rustic work, with the middle grades often the value play since a careful buyer can cut around the occasional defect.

Two further systems complete the softwood picture. Timbers, pieces five inches and thicker, are graded under their own rules, with categories like beams and stringers versus posts and timbers reflecting bending versus compression duty. And specialty products carry their own marks: finger-jointed studs are structurally rated with the added note that they must stay dry, and remanufactured or resawn lumber loses its original grade stamp, which matters because building inspectors can and do reject unstamped structural lumber. For the buyer the rule of thumb is clean: when the piece holds up a building, buy by the structural grade the plans or code demand and never sand off a stamp before inspection; when the piece decorates one, buy with your eyes, using the appearance grade as a starting sort rather than a verdict.

sections.heading: Reading a Softwood Grade Stamp
sections.body:
Every piece of structural softwood lumber sold in North America carries an ink stamp, and those few square inches encode nearly everything an inspector, engineer, or careful builder needs to know. Learning to read the stamp turns a pile of anonymous studs into documented material. A standard stamp carries five elements, though their layout varies by agency: the certification mark of the grading agency, the mill's identification number, the grade, the species or species group, and the moisture condition at the time of surfacing.

The agency mark is a logo, such as the WWPA's mark for Western mills or SPIB's for Southern pine, and it means the mill grades under that agency's supervision, with third-party oversight accredited through the American Lumber Standard Committee; the mark is what makes the stamp legally meaningful to building codes. The mill number identifies exactly which sawmill produced the piece, allowing any grading dispute to be traced to its source; a few large mills stamp a name instead.
