The grade appears as a number or abbreviation: STAND for Standard, STUD for stud grade, No 2 or the numeral 2 for Number 2, SEL STR for Select Structural, CONST for Construction, and so on, and on MSR lumber a rating like 2100f 1.8E replaces the visual grade, stating allowable bending stress and stiffness directly.

The species mark repays attention because softwood is sold in groups. D FIR or DF-L means Douglas fir and western larch, graded together because their properties are close; HEM-FIR covers western hemlock and several true firs; SPF, spruce-pine-fir, is the vast Canadian group; SYP is southern yellow pine, whose stamps often say the specific rule. Design values differ meaningfully between groups: southern pine and Douglas fir-larch are stronger than SPF grade for grade, which is why span tables list them separately and why substituting species on an engineered job needs a check. The moisture designation records the condition when the piece was planed: S-GRN means surfaced green, above nineteen percent moisture; S-DRY or KD means surfaced at nineteen percent or below; MC15 or KD15 means fifteen percent or below. Dry-stamped lumber was sized to shrink less in service, and codes and good practice prefer it for framing that will be enclosed.

Two special marks matter in trade and treatment. HT means heat treated, the pest-control cooking that international shipping rules require for solid-wood packaging and that export lumber carries; it is about insects, not strength or drying quality, though kiln-dried lumber exceeds its requirements. Pressure-treated lumber carries, in addition to its grade stamp, an end tag or label stating the preservative, the retention level, and the intended exposure, such as ground contact, and that tag, not the green tint, is what tells you the board suits the application.

A worked example ties it together. A stud stamped with the SPIB mark, mill 47, No 2, SYP, KD19 reads: graded Number 2 under Southern Pine Inspection Bureau rules at mill number 47, southern yellow pine, kiln dried to nineteen percent or less before surfacing. An inspector accepts it for any place the plans call for Number 2 southern pine or better. When you cut a stamped board, keep the stamped offcut with structural material until inspection where that matters, and when you find unstamped lumber in a structural pile, treat it as unknown wood, useful for blocking, not for the beam.

sections.heading: Defects That Decide Grade: Knots, Wane, Checks, Splits, and Warp
sections.body:
Grading, at bottom, is the systematic accounting of defects, and knowing the defects by name lets you see boards the way a grader does. The vocabulary divides into natural characteristics the tree grew, seasoning defects the drying process caused, and manufacturing defects the mill introduced.

Knots lead every list. A knot is the buried base of a branch, and its effect depends on size, location, and soundness. A sound, tight knot is intergrown with the surrounding wood and stays put; a loose or encased knot, ringed by bark, can drop out leaving a hole; a spike knot, sliced lengthwise by the saw, cuts across grain and weakens more than its area suggests. Structurally, a knot on the edge of a joist's tension face costs far more strength than the same knot at the neutral center, which is why structural rules key knot limits to position, and why you should crown and place framing so the worst edge knots land in compression. In appearance work, tight small knots may be the entire point, as in knotty pine paneling, which is a reminder that a defect is only a defect relative to a use.

Wane is missing wood along an edge or corner where the board reached the log's rounded outside, often carrying bark. It reduces the bearing and nailing surface and is limited by every grade; in rustic furniture it gets renamed live edge and priced up, the trade's best joke about the relativity of defects. Checks are separations along the grain that do not pass through the board, usually from too-fast surface drying; end checks at board ends are so routine that buyers expect to trim an inch or two, and yards wax board ends to slow them. Splits pass clear through the thickness and cost real cutting length. Shake is a separation that follows the growth rings, a failure that began in the standing tree, and it is treated harshly because it tends to extend. Pitch pockets, bark pockets, and gum streaks hold sticky or dark inclusions; decay, or rot, is disqualifying in structural grades in any active form; and insect damage ranges from pinholes, often merely cosmetic, to grub holes that gut a board's yield. Stain deserves its own note: blue-gray sapstain in pine and the mineral streaks of maple discolor without weakening, so structural rules mostly shrug at them while appearance buyers care intensely.

Warp is the geometry family, and its four members have precise names worth using. Bow is a curve along the face from end to end; crook, or spring, is a curve along the edge, the enemy of straight walls and door frames; cup is a curve across the width, the fate of wide flat-sawn boards dried unevenly; and twist is the propeller, the worst of the four because no amount of clamping truly removes it. Check every board by sighting down its length from one end, and reject twist for anything that must stay flat. Manufacturing defects complete the census: skip, where the planer missed a patch and left it rough; torn grain; machine burn; and mis-sizing.

The buyer's craft is matching defects to the cutting list. A split you will trim off costs nothing; a crook in a board you will rip into narrow strips disappears; cup in a board destined to be crosscut into short pieces mostly flattens out. The defects that should actually turn your hand away are twist, active rot, shake, and large loose knots in the middle of the lengths you need clear, because those are the ones no plan survives.

sections.heading: Moisture Content, Kiln Drying, and Wood Movement
sections.body:
Wood is hygroscopic: it takes on and gives off water with the air around it for its entire service life, swelling as it gains and shrinking as it loses, and more projects are ruined by ignoring this than by any error of strength. Moisture content, abbreviated MC, is expressed as the weight of water in a piece divided by the weight of its bone-dry wood, so freshly felled green wood can read far above one hundred percent in some species. As wood dries, free water leaves the cell cavities first with no dimensional effect; only when the cell walls themselves begin to dry, below the fiber saturation point at roughly 28 to 30 percent MC, does shrinkage begin, and from there the wood shrinks in proportion to further loss.

The destination matters more than the journey: wood in service settles toward equilibrium moisture content, the EMC dictated by the humidity around it. Outdoor air across much of North America produces an EMC around twelve to fourteen percent; heated and air-conditioned interiors run around six to nine percent, drier in winter heating. This is why the trade dries lumber to targets by use. Softwood framing is dried to nineteen percent, the S-DRY threshold, or fifteen for premium stock, because a house frame lives in a semi-protected middle world and will finish drying in place. Hardwood for furniture is kiln dried to six to eight percent, matching the interiors where furniture lives, and reputable yards store it out of the weather to keep it there. Kilns do the work in days to weeks with heat, controlled humidity, and airflow; air drying, at the old rule of a year per inch of thickness, gets wood only to outdoor EMC, which is why air-dried stock still needs acclimation or kiln finishing before fine interior work. Kiln schedules also set pests and pitch, and heat treatment for export rides on the same process.

Shrinkage is directional, and the numbers explain most warping. Along the grain, longitudinal shrinkage is negligible, a few tenths of a percent. Across the grain it is large and unequal: tangential shrinkage, along the growth rings, runs roughly six to ten percent from green to oven dry in common species, about twice the radial shrinkage across the rings, at three to five. That two-to-one ratio is why flat-sawn boards, whose faces are tangential, cup toward the bark side and move about twice as much in width as quartersawn boards, whose faces are radial; it is why quartersawn stock is specified for door stiles, instrument sides, and anything that must stay flat; and it is why a wide flat-sawn tabletop can change a quarter inch or more in width between July and January in a heated house.

Working practice follows directly. Buy dry wood in the first place, and check it: a pin or pinless moisture meter is a modest investment that settles arguments instantly, and hardwood for interior work should read six to nine percent. Acclimate lumber in the room, or at least the building, where it will live, stickered so air reaches all faces, for days to weeks depending on how far its reading stands from target. Design for movement rather than against it: fasten wide tabletops with buttons or slotted clips that let the top slide, float solid panels in frame grooves, run breadboard ends on elongated pins, and never glue or screw a wide solid panel rigidly across its grain, because when the seasons change, the wood will move, and something, joint, panel, or fastener, will lose.

sections.heading: Log Scaling: Doyle, Scribner, and International 1/4-Inch Rules
sections.body:
Before a board foot of lumber exists, someone must estimate how many board feet a log will yield, because logs are bought and sold on that estimate. The procedure is called scaling, the person is a scaler, and the formulas are log rules. All of them take the same inputs, the diameter inside bark at the small end of the log and the log's length, and predict sawn yield after accounting for the slabs, edgings, sawdust, and taper that never become lumber. Three rules dominate North American practice, they disagree substantially, and knowing which rule a price is quoted in is as important as the price.

The Doyle rule, devised in the nineteenth century and dominant in the hardwood country of the East and South, is a simple formula: subtract four inches from the small-end diameter, square the result, and multiply by the length in feet divided by sixteen. Its four-inch slab allowance is far too harsh for small logs and about right only for large ones, so Doyle famously under-scales small logs: a twelve-inch by sixteen-foot log scales just 64 board feet by Doyle when a mill can actually saw substantially more from it, while by twenty-eight or thirty inches of diameter the rule comes close to reality. Buyers quoting Doyle on small timber are, knowingly or not, buying wood the scale never counts, and sellers of small hardwood logs should understand exactly this before shaking hands.

The Scribner rule, published by J. M. Scribner in 1846, took a more honest route: diagrams of one-inch boards drawn inside circles of each diameter, with the resulting yields collected into tables, later regularized as Scribner Decimal C, which rounds to the nearest ten board feet. Scribner ignores taper, crediting nothing for the wood a long log gains toward its butt, so it too runs conservative, especially on long logs, but far less brutally than Doyle on small ones. It remains standard in much of the West and in public timber sales in various regions. The International rule, developed by Judson Clark in 1900 and issued in its quarter-inch kerf version in 1906, is the most accurate of the three: built from a mathematical model of sawing that allows for a quarter-inch saw kerf, shrinkage, and, crucially, log taper at half an inch of diameter per four feet of length, it tracks modern mill recovery closely enough that foresters use it as the benchmark against which the others' biases are measured. The United States Forest Service has long used International quarter-inch widely in the East, and growth-and-yield research generally speaks it.

The differences are not academic. That twelve-inch sixteen-footer scales roughly 64 board feet Doyle, about 80 Scribner, and about 95 International; a twenty-inch log narrows the spread; a thirty-inch log nearly closes it. Mills track overrun, the percentage by which actual lumber output exceeds log scale, and overrun of thirty to fifty percent against Doyle on small logs is unremarkable, while against International a good mill runs near even. Consequently, timber buyers, landowners selling stumpage, and sawyers negotiating custom milling should always name the rule, and when comparing prices convert to one rule first. Beyond the big three, regional and historical rules persist, and outside North America logs trade in cubic meters, a reminder that the board-foot log rule is a cultural artifact of American sawmilling, with all the charm and friction that implies. For a landowner, the practical advice is blunt: get the scale in writing, know the rule, and remember that the small logs the Doyle scale dismisses still saw into real lumber.

sections.heading: Buying Lumber: Pricing per Board Foot, Waste Factors, and Project Estimates
sections.body:
Estimating a project in board feet is the skill that keeps woodworking on budget, and it is mostly disciplined bookkeeping. Start from your cutting list: every part's final thickness, width, and length. Convert each part to board feet using its final dimensions, sum them, and you have the net wood in the finished piece. That number is never what you buy. Between the rack and the finished project stand the planer shavings that take rough stock to final thickness, the jointer passes that straighten edges, the trim cuts that remove end checks and snipe, the rips that waste kerf, the defects you cut around, and the parts you spoil and remake. The allowance for all of it is the waste factor, and experienced makers add fifteen to thirty percent for straightforward work in upper-grade lumber, forty percent or more when working Common grades, highly figured stock, or designs with wide clear panels, and closer to double for chairs and curved work where parts nest badly in boards.

Grade selection is the biggest cost lever you control. Price the same project two ways: FAS at the premium with a modest waste factor, and Number 1 Common at its discount with a heavier factor, and let your longest required clear cutting decide. If nothing on your list exceeds three feet clear, the Common pile usually wins decisively; if the design needs eight clear feet, only the upper grades can promise it. Species choice moves cost even more, and within a species, thickness does: 8/4 stock costs meaningfully more per board foot than 4/4, so resawing thick stock to yield thin parts only pays when you need matched faces. Remember also the tally conventions working quietly against you: hardwood billed at rough quarter thickness though delivered surfaced thinner, softwood billed at nominal dimension, and random widths meaning you buy the board that exists, not the width you drew.

At the yard, the workflow is simple and worth ritualizing. Bring the cutting list and a tape. Sight every board down its length for twist and crook; check ends for splits and the faces for the defects your parts cannot tolerate; measure and tally as you stack, keeping your own running total to compare against the counter's. Ask prices before sorting, since many yards price by grade and thickness per species on a posted sheet, and ask about quantity breaks, shorts bins, and skip-planed stock, where bargains live. For softwood dimension lumber the same habits apply with the arithmetic simplified by uniform sizes: count pieces, multiply by board feet per piece, and mind that per-piece retail pricing often diverges from any per-board-foot logic, so compare the sizes you could substitute.

The worked example below shows the whole chain for a bookcase in cherry, and the steps condense the estimating procedure for any project. Suppose the case needs two sides at 0.75 by 11.25 inches by 6 feet, five shelves at 0.75 by 11 inches by 3 feet, and a face frame totaling 8 linear feet of 0.75 by 2 inch stock. Net board feet: sides about 11.3, shelves about 13.8, frame about 1.3, call it 26.4 net. In 4/4 FAS at nine dollars with twenty percent waste, buy about 32 board feet for roughly 290 dollars; in Number 1 Common at five and a half with thirty-five percent waste, buy about 36 board feet for under 200, provided the 6-foot sides can be found clear in the pile, which is exactly the judgment call the grades exist to inform.
steps: Write a complete cutting list with each part's final thickness, width, and length, and convert every part to board feet using the formula.
Sum the parts to get net board feet, then group parts by the rough thickness they must be cut from, assigning each group a quarter size.
Identify your longest and widest required clear cutting, and choose the lowest grade whose typical yield can supply it.
Apply a waste factor to each thickness group: 15 to 30 percent for upper grades and simple designs, 35 percent or more for Common grades, figure, or curved work.
Price the total at the yard's per-board-foot rates, comparing at least two grade scenarios before deciding.
At the yard, sight each board for twist and crook, check for splits and disqualifying defects, and keep your own tally as you stack.
Buy slightly long on your estimate rather than planning a return trip, since matching color and grain from a later batch is rarely possible.

sections.heading: Sheet Goods, Linear Feet, Cords, and Other Ways Wood Is Sold
sections.body:
The board foot rules solid sawn lumber, but a great deal of the wood you will buy is measured by other conventions, and mixing them up is a classic estimating error. Sheet goods come first. Plywood, MDF, particleboard, and OSB are sold by the sheet, with the four-by-eight-foot panel, 32 square feet, as the standard, and thickness quoted separately. Like softwood lumber, panels have their own nominal-actual gap: a three-quarter-inch hardwood plywood panel commonly measures 23/32 of an inch, and imported panels are often metric, 18 millimeters standing in for three quarters, which matters the moment you cut a dado sized from the name rather than the caliper. Hardwood plywood carries a face-grading system of its own, letters for the face veneer, A best, and numbers for the back, so a panel graded A1 has premium faces both sides while C3 is shop grade; construction panels use their own letter pairs, like AC or CDX, where X marks exterior-rated glue. Comparing plywood to solid stock per square foot of usable surface is often eye-opening in plywood's favor for casework, which is exactly why cabinets are built from it.

Linear-foot pricing covers anything sold by length alone at a fixed profile: mouldings, trim, dowels, handrail, and often live-edge slabs' poor cousin, the dressed S4S hobby boards racked at home centers. A crown moulding at three dollars a linear foot costs the same per foot whether the profile is pine or primed MDF composite, so compare profiles and materials, not just rates, and note that home-center S4S hardwood by the linear foot usually works out to two or three times the per-board-foot price of the same species rough at a hardwood dealer, the premium buying convenience and small quantities. Slabs and figured stock frequently abandon volume pricing altogether and sell by the piece, priced on beauty; there the board-foot math serves only as your sanity check on what the beauty premium actually is.

Firewood and pulpwood use bulk measures. The cord is a stacked volume of 128 cubic feet, the traditional four-by-four-by-eight-foot pile, and because stacking includes air, a cord contains perhaps 80 to 90 cubic feet of actual wood; a face cord or rick is a four-by-eight face of shorter sticks, a third to half a cord depending on stick length, and sellers quoting face cords without stating stick length are quoting fog. Pulpwood and chips trade by the ton, green or dry, and industrial roundwood internationally trades in cubic meters, the measure nearly every country outside North America uses for logs and sawn timber alike; one cubic meter equals about 424 board feet by straight conversion, though log-rule quirks make real-world equivalences messier.

A few unit translations complete the toolkit. A board foot is one twelfth of a cubic foot, so a cubic foot holds twelve board feet. A thousand board feet, the MBF of commodity quotes, is about 2.36 cubic meters. A four-by-eight sheet of three-quarter plywood contains the volume equivalent of about 21 board feet, useful when comparing panel and solid options for the same casework. And when a deal is quoted in an unfamiliar unit, the universal defense is the same one this guide has urged throughout: convert everything to one measure, price it there, and only then compare. Wood is sold in more dialects than any other building material; the buyer who speaks board feet, sheets, linear feet, and cords fluently is the one the market cannot confuse.

sections.heading: Putting It Together: From Log to Project, a Working Fluency
sections.body:
Everything in this guide converges into a single working fluency, and it is worth walking the whole chain once to see how the pieces mesh. A tree is felled and bucked into logs; a scaler measures small-end diameter and length and applies a log rule, Doyle, Scribner, or International quarter-inch, to predict the board feet inside, and money changes hands on that estimate. The sawmill breaks the log down, chasing yield: flat sawing for speed and width, quartersawing some species for stability and figure, and the mill's recovery against log scale, the overrun, is its margin. The green boards are stickered, air dried or kiln dried to a target moisture content matched to their destiny, nineteen percent or less for framing softwood, six to eight for furniture hardwood, then surfaced. Softwood emerges in standardized nominal sizes with actual dressed dimensions fixed by the softwood standard, is graded visually or by machine for strength, and takes an ink stamp recording agency, mill, grade, species group, and dryness. Hardwood emerges in random widths and lengths, tallied in rough quarter thicknesses, and is graded under NHLA rules by predicted clear-cutting yield into FAS, Selects, and the Commons. Both streams flow through wholesalers to yards, where retail sorting, surfacing, and marketing overlay the formal grades.

The buyer meets this river at the rack, and every skill in this guide is a form of respect for what the material has already been through. Reading a grade stamp tells you what an inspector will accept and what an engineer assumed. Reading a hardwood pile through half-closed eyes, as a grader would, tells you what yield the price actually buys. The board-foot formula converts any pile into a number, and the number into a bill, before the counter does it for you. The quarter system tells you what rough thickness to buy so that your finished part emerges from it with cleanup to spare. The defect vocabulary sorts the boards that will fight you, twist, shake, rot, loose knots amidships, from the ones whose flaws your cutting list will simply excise. The moisture meter and a week of acclimation protect a winter's work from a summer's humidity. And the waste factor, honestly applied, is the difference between one trip to the yard and an apologetic second one hunting for color-matched boards that no longer exist.

A few habits compound all of it. Keep a notebook, paper or phone, of what you paid per board foot, per species, per grade, per yard, because lumber prices move and memory flatters; a year of entries makes you the best-informed buyer in the store. Build relationships: small yards and sawyers will call you when something special hits the deck, will let you into the back stacks once you have shown you restack neatly, and will explain their own tally conventions if asked plainly. Buy ahead for wood you know you will use, since dry, stickered storage in your own shop is the cheapest kiln and the best hedge, and well-kept stock only gets more acclimated. When a deal seems too good, scale it yourself, check the rule, check the tally, check the moisture, and usually you will find the catch; occasionally you will find a bargain, and you will have earned it. The measurement and grading systems in this guide were built over more than a century precisely so that strangers could trade a natural, variable material fairly. Learn their language, and the trade treats you as a native; ignore it, and you pay tourist prices for the rest of your woodworking life.

guides.safetyNote: Lumber work carries real physical hazards even before a saw is switched on. Boards are heavy, long, and awkward: lift with your legs, get help or use a cart for anything over arm's length, and watch both ends in aisles and doorways. Rough-sawn lumber gives splinters, so wear gloves when handling it, and stacked boards can shift or fall, so never pull from the middle of a pile. Lumberyards run forklifts in tight quarters; stay visible and out of their lanes. If you mill or cut wood, use eye and hearing protection, keep guards in place, and collect or mask against wood dust, which is a respiratory irritant and a listed carcinogen with long exposure. Treated lumber should never be burned, and its dust should not be inhaled.

guides.title: Quartersawn, Riftsawn and Flatsawn Boards
guides.summary: How a log is sliced into boards determines how the wood will move, split, wear and look, and this guide explains the flatsawn, riftsawn and quartersawn cuts from the cell wall outward. It covers ring angles, shrinkage anisotropy, mill practice, yield and price, species differences, and how to choose a cut for a given piece of work.

sections.heading: Why the Direction of the Cut Decides What a Board Will Do
sections.body:
Two boards can come from the same tree, be planed to the same thickness, carry the same species name on the invoice and behave like entirely different materials. One stays flat for forty years under a window; the other cups into a shallow gutter the first humid August and opens a crack along a glue line by Christmas. The difference is almost never the species and almost always the geometry of the cut: the angle at which the sawblade crossed the tree's annual growth rings. That angle is the single most useful thing to know about a board, and it is legible on the end grain of every piece of solid wood ever milled.

Wood is not a uniform solid. It is a bundle of long hollow cells, overwhelmingly aligned with the trunk, bound into concentric annual layers and pierced radially by sheets of storage tissue called rays. That architecture is directional, so the material's properties are directional too. Wood swells and shrinks with moisture roughly twice as much around the rings as it does across them, and almost not at all along the grain. A board whose face happens to lie tangent to the rings therefore changes width nearly twice as fast as a board whose face lies on a radius of the log. Everything that follows from that ratio — cupping, cracking at a fastener, a drawer that binds only in July, a floorboard that opens a hairline gap every winter — is a consequence of which way the saw went.

The trade names for the three basic outcomes are flatsawn (also called plainsawn or, in Britain, through-and-through or slash-sawn), quartersawn, and riftsawn. They are not three separate manufacturing processes so much as three regions of a continuum, described by the angle between the growth rings and the wide face of the board. Flatsawn boards have rings meeting the face at a shallow angle, conventionally under about thirty degrees. Quartersawn boards have rings meeting the face steeply, conventionally sixty degrees or more, ideally at ninety. Riftsawn occupies the band between, roughly thirty to sixty degrees. A single wide board cut across a log can begin as quartersawn at one edge and end as riftsawn or nearly flatsawn at the other, which is why the categories describe tendencies rather than absolutes.

Understanding these three words converts a great deal of woodworking folklore into predictable engineering. It explains why a Victorian oak library is full of ray-flecked panels, why a guitar top is split rather than sawn, why timber-frame posts are boxed heart, why exterior window sashes were traditionally specified as vertical grain, and why a cheap tabletop from a discount store telegraphs every glue joint after one heating season. It also explains price: the cuts differ in how much of a log they waste, and waste is what a lumber buyer actually pays for.

sections.heading: Inside the Log: Rings, Rays, Earlywood and Latewood
sections.body:
A tree trunk grows outward from a thin sheath of dividing cells, the vascular cambium, lying just under the bark. Each season the cambium lays down new conducting and supporting cells on its inner face, forming wood, and new food-conducting tissue on its outer face, forming inner bark. In climates with a distinct growing season the wood formed early in the year differs visibly from that formed late. Earlywood, sometimes called springwood, is made of large thin-walled cells optimised for moving water; it is pale, soft and low in density. Latewood, or summerwood, is made of smaller thick-walled cells optimised for strength; it is darker, harder and considerably denser. The abrupt boundary where one year's dense latewood meets the next year's soft earlywood is what the eye reads as a growth ring. In tropical species without a marked dry or cold season, rings may be faint, irregular or absent altogether, which is why teak and mahogany show far less dramatic figure differences between cuts than oak or Douglas fir.

Running perpendicular to those rings, like spokes on a wheel, are the rays. Rays are ribbons of parenchyma cells, one to many cells wide and several to hundreds of cells tall, that store starch and move nutrients horizontally between the outer sapwood and the interior. In most species the rays are microscopic. In a handful — white oak, red oak, sycamore and London plane, beech, some she-oaks — they are enormous, several millimetres tall and visible without a lens. When a saw cut runs parallel to those tall rays, it slices them lengthwise and exposes their broad flat faces, producing the shining silvery patches called ray fleck, medullary fleck, or in the sycamore trade simply lace. This is the single most reliable visual signature of a quartersawn board in a ray-prominent species.

Two further zones matter to a sawyer. Sapwood is the outer, still-living region that conducts water; it is usually paler, higher in starch, more attractive to fungi and insects, and in most species less durable. Heartwood is the inner core in which the cells have died and become impregnated with extractives — tannins, resins, oils and phenolics — that give walnut, cedar and white oak their colour and their decay resistance. At the very centre lies the pith, a small core of soft, weak tissue formed when the stem was a seedling shoot. The pith and the first few rings around it, called juvenile wood, have markedly different properties from mature wood: longer shrinkage along the grain, lower stiffness, and a strong tendency to twist. This is why boards containing the pith split and warp so persistently, and why a careful sawyer either boxes the pith safely inside a heavy timber or rejects it from thin stock entirely.

sections.heading: Defining the Three Cuts by Ring Angle
sections.body:
Look at the end of any board and you will see the growth rings as a set of arcs or lines. The angle those arcs make with the wide face of the board is the defining measurement, and the whole vocabulary of flatsawn, riftsawn and quartersawn is simply three bands along that one number. In North American practice the common convention is that a face grain angle of zero to thirty degrees is flatsawn or plainsawn; thirty to sixty degrees is riftsawn; and sixty to ninety degrees is quartersawn. European and British specifications often use the same bands under different names, and the softwood trades frequently use a coarser two-way split: flat grain versus vertical grain, with the boundary drawn at forty-five degrees. North American softwood grading rules for vertical grain material typically require rings at forty-five degrees or steeper and often specify a minimum ring count per inch as well, since slow growth and steep rings tend to travel together.

The visual consequence on the board's face follows directly from the geometry. When the blade runs tangent to the rings, it slices through the layered cone shapes of successive years' growth at a shallow angle and produces the familiar cathedral or flame figure: nested arches marching down the board, wide and open where the cut was shallowest. This is flatsawn timber, and its cathedral pattern is the look most people picture when they think of wood. When the blade runs along a radius, it crosses ring after ring almost head-on and produces straight parallel stripes running the length of the board, sometimes called vertical grain, comb grain, or in flooring, edge grain. Riftsawn material shows the same straight stripes but without the ray fleck, because the cut angle no longer runs along the rays.

An important subtlety is that these categories are properties of a location within the log, not of a whole board. A three-hundred-millimetre wide board taken from near the centre of a log may be steeply quartered at one edge and nearly flat at the other, because the rings curve. Wide quartersawn boards are therefore intrinsically hard to obtain: to keep the ring angle above sixty degrees across a wide face you need a large-diameter log, because the rings must be nearly straight across the board's width, and rings are only near-straight far from the pith. A common rule of thumb is that the widest genuinely quartersawn board a log can yield is roughly one quarter to one third of the log's diameter.

When buying, treat the printed category as a claim about a tendency and verify it yourself on the end grain. Sellers describe as quartersawn a great deal of material that a strict grader would call rift, and describe as rift a great deal that is really flat with a steep edge. Nothing about this is dishonest in most cases; it reflects that the categories are bands on a continuum and that boards are rarely uniform across their width.

sections.heading: Moisture, Shrinkage and the Anisotropy of Wood
sections.body:
Wood in a living tree is saturated: water fills the hollow cell cavities as free water and also saturates the cell walls themselves as bound water. When timber dries, the free water leaves first and nothing dimensional happens. The point at which the cavities are empty but the walls are still saturated is called the fibre saturation point, and it falls near twenty-eight to thirty percent moisture content by oven-dry weight for most species. Only below that point does the wood begin to shrink, because only then does water start leaving the cell walls themselves, allowing the cellulose microfibrils to draw closer together. Every dimensional problem in woodworking lives below the fibre saturation point.

The shrinkage that follows is strikingly unequal in the three directions. Along the grain, longitudinal shrinkage from green to oven-dry is typically only 0.1 to 0.2 percent — small enough that woodworkers treat length as fixed. Across the rings, in the radial direction, shrinkage is generally around 3 to 5 percent. Around the rings, in the tangential direction, it is roughly 6 to 10 percent. The ratio of tangential to radial shrinkage, usually written T/R, is the number that governs everything. For most temperate hardwoods and softwoods T/R lies between 1.5 and 2.0. Some species are much worse: hickory and pecan can approach 2.0 or beyond, and beech is notoriously unstable at around 1.9. Some are much better: mahogany and teak sit near 1.2 to 1.3, which is a large part of why those woods earned their reputation for staying put.

Concrete published figures make the point. American white oak shrinks about 5.6 percent radially and 10.5 percent tangentially, a T/R near 1.9. Black cherry is about 3.7 radial and 7.1 tangential. Sugar maple runs 4.8 and 9.9. Douglas fir, coast type, is about 4.8 and 7.6. Honduran mahogany is roughly 3.0 and 4.1. These are green-to-oven-dry totals; in service, wood swings over a much smaller band, but the ratio between the two directions holds.

For estimating real movement, a practical approximation is that wood changes dimension by about one-thirtieth of its total green-to-ovendry shrinkage for each one percent change in moisture content below the fibre saturation point. A three-hundred-millimetre-wide flatsawn white oak panel moving from six percent moisture in a heated winter house to twelve percent in a humid summer changes tangentially by roughly 300 × 0.105 × (6/30), which is about 6.3 millimetres. The same panel cut quartersawn, moving radially, changes by roughly 300 × 0.056 × (6/30), about 3.4 millimetres. Nearly half. That single arithmetic difference is the whole practical argument for quartersawn stock, and it is why a breadboard end, a floating panel or an oversized screw slot exists in traditional joinery at all.

The cause of the anisotropy is not fully settled, but the dominant explanations are the restraining effect of the rays, which run radially and resist radial swelling like reinforcing rods, and the differing behaviour of the dense latewood bands, which shrink more than earlywood and drag the softer layers with them tangentially.

sections.heading: Cupping, Bowing, Twisting and Diamonding: How Boards Distort
sections.body:
When a board dries, every part of it tries to shrink by the amount appropriate to its own local grain direction. Because those directions vary across the board, the shrinkage is uneven, and the board changes shape rather than simply getting smaller. The classic distortions each have a name and each has a straightforward geometric cause.

Cup is the across-the-width curvature that turns a flat board into a shallow trough. It is the signature defect of flatsawn timber, and it happens because the face nearer the bark has rings closer to tangent and therefore shrinks more in width than the face nearer the pith, whose rings are more steeply inclined. The board becomes a segment of a shrinking ring, and the classic mnemonic is that the rings try to straighten out: the concave side of the cup faces away from the pith, so the growth-ring arcs on the end grain flatten. A useful practical corollary is that in a wide flatsawn plank the bark side is the side that goes hollow. Quartersawn stock is nearly immune to cup, because shrinkage across its width is uniformly radial on both faces.

Bow is curvature along the length in the face plane, and crook, also called spring or edge bend, is curvature along the length in the edge plane. Both usually arise from longitudinal shrinkage differences: a board containing juvenile wood, reaction wood or a section of the pith has zones whose along-the-grain shrinkage is many times normal, and the board bends toward the shorter side. Reaction wood is a particular culprit. Leaning conifers form dense, resin-rich compression wood on the underside of the lean, which shrinks longitudinally up to ten times more than normal wood; leaning hardwoods form tension wood on the upper side, which does the same and also machines with a woolly, torn surface no amount of sharpening quite cures.

Twist, sometimes called wind or warp in the propeller sense, comes chiefly from spiral grain, where the tree's fibres corkscrew around the trunk rather than running straight up it. Since longitudinal shrinkage is tiny but tangential is large, fibres that run diagonally across the board's face drag one corner more than the other as they dry. Spiral grain is heritable and species-typical; some plantations of fast-grown pine are notorious for it.

Diamonding is the distortion of a square section into a rhombus, and it happens when the diagonal of the section runs tangentially while the other runs radially. It is why a truly square, truly stable table leg is best cut riftsawn, so that the rings run diagonally corner to corner and both faces shrink at the same intermediate rate.

Finally there is case-hardening and honeycombing, which are drying faults rather than cut faults: an over-fast schedule dries the shell before the core, the shell sets in tension, and the board later pinches the saw or splits internally. No cut geometry protects against a bad kiln schedule.

sections.heading: Reading the End Grain: Identifying What You Have
sections.body:
The most valuable skill in this whole subject takes about ten seconds per board and requires no tools. Square the end of the board or plane a small facet on it, hold it to a raking light, and look at the growth rings as lines. Estimate the angle those lines make with the wide face. If they lie nearly flat along the face, sweeping into arcs, the board is flatsawn. If they stand nearly perpendicular, crossing from face to face like the pages of a closed book, it is quartersawn. If they run diagonally, at somewhere near forty-five degrees, it is riftsawn. Check both edges of a wide board separately, because a wide board frequently changes category across its width.

There are useful secondary confirmations. Ray fleck on the face is close to conclusive evidence of quartersawn material in oak, sycamore, plane, beech and lacewood, because those broad silvery patches only appear when the cut is nearly parallel to the rays; the fleck fades and vanishes as you rotate toward rift. A cathedral or flame pattern on the face is conclusive evidence of flatsawn material, since those nested arches are the intersection of a shallow plane with the cone-shaped growth surfaces. Perfectly straight parallel stripes with no fleck and no arches strongly suggests rift. Counting rings across a face is also informative: on a quartersawn face you cross many rings in a short distance, typically as a dense stripe pattern, whereas a flatsawn face can show only two or three rings across its whole width.

Beware of two traps. First, a board can be resawn or planed after milling so that the face you are shown is not the original sawn face; only the end grain tells the truth. Second, many boards are sold with one good face. A board quartersawn on the face you are shown may be rift or flat on the other, especially if it came from near the pith. If both faces matter — a table leaf, a door panel, an exposed shelf — check both.

For flooring and softwood, the trade often uses the shorthand vertical grain versus flat grain, and grading rules put numbers on it. Typical vertical grain softwood grading requires rings at forty-five degrees or steeper to the face across a stated proportion of the width, and premium grades may additionally require a minimum of six to eight rings per inch, about two to three per centimetre, which excludes fast-grown plantation stock.

One last diagnostic worth knowing is the pith test. If you can see the pith itself, or the tight, strongly curved rings immediately around it, reject the board for anything that must stay flat. Juvenile wood near the pith has abnormal longitudinal shrinkage and will bow or check no matter how it was sawn.

sections.heading: Ray Fleck, Silver Grain and the Figure of Quartersawn Wood
sections.body:
The decorative reputation of quartersawn timber rests almost entirely on the rays. In species where the rays are tall enough to see, cutting parallel to them exposes broad flat sheets of tissue whose cells are oriented crosswise to the surrounding fibres. Light striking that sheet reflects differently from light striking the surrounding longitudinal fibres, so the patches flash silver at one viewing angle and go dark at another. The trade calls the effect ray fleck, silver grain, medullary figure, or in the plane-tree trade, lacewood. It is chatoyant, meaning it changes with viewing angle, and photographs poorly for exactly that reason.

White oak is the classic. Quercus alba and its European cousin Quercus robur have rays that can be twenty to fifty millimetres tall and several cells wide, producing the large irregular flakes that define Arts and Crafts, Mission and much Gothic Revival furniture. Gustav Stickley's workshops after 1900 built an entire visual identity on quartersawn white oak with a fumed ammonia finish, and Frank Lloyd Wright specified it constantly. Red oak has rays too, but shorter and less dramatic, so its quartered figure is a finer pinstripe. Sycamore and London plane have very regular, closely spaced rays that on the quarter produce the dense freckled lacewood pattern beloved of Art Deco cabinetmakers; the same timber flatsawn is an unremarkable pale board. Beech shows a fine dash-like fleck. Silky oak, she-oak and Australian lacewood are prized for the same reason.

Several other figure types are often confused with ray fleck but come from different causes and are largely independent of the cut. Curl or fiddleback figure, seen in maple, is a wavy undulation of the fibres themselves, and it shows best on the flatsawn or slightly rift face; quartersawing curly maple can actually mute it. Quilt, blister and pommele are three-dimensional bulges in the fibre alignment and are usually best displayed flatsawn or rotary cut. Bird's-eye maple comes from small conical dimples in the grain and is likewise a flatsawn effect. Interlocked grain in mahogany, sapele and many tropical species, where fibres reverse spiral direction every few years, produces the ribbon or stripe figure — and that one is genuinely a quartersawn effect, since only a radial cut crosses the alternating layers to make the alternating light and dark bands.

There is a practical trade-off hidden in the aesthetics. Ray fleck is a plane of weakness. Large flakes are essentially sheets of short, crosswise cells embedded in a matrix of long ones, and they can lift, tear out under a plane iron, or flake off along their own plane in service. In heavily flecked oak, plane with a very sharp, finely set iron, take light cuts, and expect some scraping or sanding to be necessary where a flake meets the surface at a shallow angle. Some finishers deliberately choose thin penetrating oils over film finishes on flecked oak because a film sitting over a partially lifted flake looks cloudy.

sections.heading: How a Sawmill Actually Cuts a Log
sections.body:
Almost nobody actually cuts a log into true radial slices, because doing so would produce a heap of wedges and very few rectangular boards. What mills do instead is choose among a small family of patterns, each trading yield against ring angle. Knowing the patterns explains both the price list and why a board looks the way it does.

Through-and-through sawing, also called live sawing or boule sawing, simply runs the log past the blade in parallel passes without turning it. It is the fastest, highest-yield method and the one a portable bandmill operator uses by default. The stack that comes off is a boule: the outer boards are nearly flatsawn, the boards near the centre are nearly quartersawn, and everything in between graduates through rift. Keeping the boule in order is valuable because adjacent boards book-match beautifully.

Plainsawing, sometimes called cant sawing or grade sawing, is the industrial workhorse. The sawyer takes a few boards off one face, rotates the log ninety degrees, takes a few more, and continues around, chasing the best grade on each fresh face. Most boards come out flatsawn, with rift material appearing near the corners. Quartersawing proper requires cutting the log into quarters first and then slicing each quarter, re-orienting between cuts to keep the blade near a radius. Rift sawing in its strict sense is more demanding still, rotating the quarter slightly after every single board so that the cut always runs on a true radius; it is the lowest-yield and most expensive method of all, which is why most commercial rift lumber is really a by-product of quartersawing rather than a deliberate pattern.

The steps below describe a realistic small-mill quartersawing sequence on a bandsaw mill, the kind that produces genuine quartered oak in a one-person operation.
steps: Select a log at least 400 mm in diameter at the small end, straight, with no visible sweep and minimal taper; small logs cannot yield wide quartered boards because their rings curve too tightly.
Cut the log to length and remove any flare or buttress at the butt so it will sit stably in the mill's dogs.
Slab off one face flat, roll the log ninety degrees, and slab the adjacent face so you have a stable right-angled reference.
Saw the log in half through the pith, then saw each half through the pith again, producing four quarters each with a ninety-degree corner at the pith.
Mount one quarter with a flat face down and the pith corner pointing away from you.
Take a board off the face, then rotate the quarter ninety degrees onto its other flat face and take a board from that face.
Continue alternating faces, keeping the cut near a radius on every board and producing the classic stepped profile on the remaining wedge.
Set aside the narrow triangular offcuts near the pith; discard any board that contains pith or the first two or three rings around it.
Edge each board to remove bark, wane and sapwood, keeping the widest yield consistent with a ring angle above sixty degrees.
Sticker the stack immediately, within hours, since freshly quartered faces check quickly.

sections.heading: Yield, Waste and Why Quartersawn Costs More
sections.body:
Quartersawn lumber typically costs anywhere from thirty percent to well over double the price of the same species and grade flatsawn. The premium is not a fashion markup; it is arithmetic about what leaves the mill as saleable board and what leaves as sawdust and firewood.

A through-and-through or plainsawn pattern converts a large fraction of the log's cross-section into rectangles, because parallel cuts across a circle waste only the four curved segments at the edges. Typical lumber recovery for plainsawing a good hardwood log runs somewhere in the region of sixty to seventy percent of the log's board volume. Quartersawing replaces those parallel cuts with a pattern that must repeatedly approach the pith at an angle, so a great deal of the log ends as narrow triangular offcuts near the centre and short, tapering pieces near the circumference. Recovery drops, commonly quoted in the region of forty to fifty percent, and true rift sawing lower still.

Three further costs compound the yield loss. First, handling time: quartersawing requires the log to be turned and re-dogged after almost every cut, which can double or triple the sawyer's minutes per cubic metre. Second, board width: since ring angle degrades as a board widens, quartered boards come off narrower on average, and narrow boards fetch a lower price per unit volume in every grading system in the world while requiring more glue joints from the buyer. Third, log selection: only large, straight, defect-free logs are worth quartersawing at all, so the input log itself is a premium purchase. A mill that quartersaws a mediocre log has spent premium sawing time to make cheap boards.

Against that, quartered stock carries real offsetting value. It dries faster and more evenly because moisture moves more readily along the rays, so kiln schedules can sometimes be shortened; it degrades less in the kiln, with far less cup and surface checking, so the proportion of the dried stack that downgrades is smaller; and it commands a premium in applications where stability is worth paying for, notably flooring, exterior joinery, musical instruments, boatbuilding and fine furniture.

There is also a genuine sustainability argument that cuts both ways. Quartersawing wastes more of each log, which is bad; but quartersawn products last longer in service and are less likely to be scrapped for distortion, which is good. For a reader buying small quantities, the practical arbitrage is worth knowing: buy a through-and-through boule from a small mill and you will get the quartersawn centre boards at flatsawn prices, because you are buying the whole log rather than asking the mill to sort. Many small woodworkers acquire almost all of their quartered stock this way.

sections.heading: Riftsawn: The Overlooked Middle Ground
sections.body:
Riftsawn material sits between the other two and is chronically misunderstood, partly because the word is used in at least three incompatible ways. In the strictest mill sense, rift sawing is a specific cutting pattern in which every board is taken on a true radius by rotating the quarter after each cut. In the common lumberyard sense, riftsawn simply describes any board whose ring angle falls in the thirty-to-sixty-degree band. In a third usage, particularly in the oak trade, riftsawn means quartersawn-without-the-fleck: boards whose rings are steep enough to be stable but whose cut angle misses the rays, so they show clean straight stripes and no flakes.

That third meaning captures why rift material is prized in certain traditions. A great deal of mid-century modern and contemporary Scandinavian-influenced furniture uses riftsawn white oak precisely because it reads as calm and linear: the straight parallel stripes give the visual discipline of quartersawn without the busy flash of ray fleck that reads as Victorian or Arts and Crafts. Architects specifying oak panelling for a minimalist interior almost always mean rift, whatever word they write.

Structurally, rift stock has one clear and underappreciated advantage: it is the correct cut for square sections. A square leg cut with the rings running diagonally corner to corner shrinks by an intermediate, roughly equal amount on both faces, so it stays square. A square leg cut flatsawn shrinks much more in one direction than the other and becomes a rectangle; cut with the rings parallel to two faces, it can diamond noticeably. Traditional chairmakers and table makers select rift stock for legs and stiles for exactly this reason, and a leg cut from the corner of a quartered log will conveniently show straight grain on all four faces, which is visually valuable in a leg seen from every side.

Rift's practical drawback is availability and price. Because strict rift sawing is the lowest-yield pattern of all, commercial rift material is largely a by-product: the boards taken from the corners of a plainsawn cant, or the off-angle boards from a quartersawing run. A yard that sells rift oak is usually selling a sorted subset of its own quarter-sawing output, and the price is generally at or above quartersawn. Widths are typically narrow, often under 150 millimetres, because the angle band is narrow.

For dimensional stability rift sits, unsurprisingly, in between. Its movement in width is intermediate between radial and tangential, closer to radial as the angle steepens. A useful approximation is that the effective shrinkage coefficient interpolates roughly with the sine of the ring angle, so a forty-five-degree board moves at close to the average of the species' radial and tangential figures. For most temperate hardwoods that means roughly three quarters of the movement of flatsawn stock and a quarter more than quartersawn — a real improvement, if not the full benefit.

sections.heading: Species Differences and Where the Rules Bend
sections.body:
The general principles hold across all timber, but the size of the benefit varies enormously by species, and in a few cases the usual advice inverts. The controlling variables are the tangential-to-radial shrinkage ratio, the size of the rays, and whether the species has interlocked or figured grain.

Species where quartersawing pays the largest dividend are those with a high T/R ratio and prominent rays. White and red oak lead the list, with T/R near 1.8 to 1.9 and visible fleck; beech is even more unstable, with a notorious reputation for movement that makes flatsawn beech a poor choice for anything wide; sycamore and London plane have moderate ratios but spectacular quartered figure; hickory and pecan have very high ratios and benefit greatly. Douglas fir and southern yellow pine both show a marked practical difference, which is why vertical grain fir was the standard specification for flooring, window sash and boat decking for a century.

Species where the benefit is smaller are those already dimensionally calm. Genuine mahogany, teak, Spanish cedar and black walnut all have relatively low T/R ratios in the 1.2 to 1.6 range, so flatsawn boards of these species are far more trustworthy than flatsawn oak. Teak's combination of low ratio and high oil content is much of the reason it dominated boatbuilding. Where those species are quartersawn, the reason is usually figure — mahogany and sapele are quartersawn to bring out ribbon stripe from interlocked grain — rather than stability.

Two important exceptions run the other way. First, some highly figured woods look better flatsawn: curly and quilted maple, bird's-eye maple, and burl display their figure on the tangential face and can be visually flattened by quartering. Second, interlocked tropical species can be difficult to plane on the quarter precisely because the alternating fibre direction means half the surface is being cut against the grain no matter which way the plane travels; a scraper, a very high cutting angle, or sanding is often necessary on quartered sapele and iroko.

A special case worth knowing is riven rather than sawn wood. Splitting a log with a froe and wedges follows the natural fibre planes rather than cutting across them, so riven stock is by definition radial and has unbroken continuous fibres running its whole length. This makes it dramatically stronger in bending than any sawn equivalent, which is why traditional chair spindles, ladder rungs, basket splints, shingles, barrel staves and cleft-oak fencing are riven. A riven oak stave and a sawn oak stave of identical dimensions are not equivalent products; the sawn one will have grain run-out where the blade crossed fibres and can fail at a fraction of the load.

sections.heading: Choosing a Cut for the Job
sections.body:
The right cut depends on what the piece must do, and the honest answer is often that it does not matter much. For small parts, narrow parts, and anything under about 75 millimetres wide, seasonal movement is measured in tenths of a millimetre and any cut will serve. The decision starts to matter when a piece is wide, when it is constrained by fasteners or joinery, when it is exposed to swinging humidity, or when appearance is the point.

For a wide solid tabletop, quartersawn or rift stock reduces movement by roughly half and greatly reduces the risk of cupping, but it is expensive and often unavailable in wide boards. The traditional compromise is to build the top from several narrower flatsawn boards with the growth-ring arcs alternating from board to board, so that whatever cupping occurs is subdivided into small opposing curves rather than one large one; opinions on alternating rings differ, and some makers prefer to orient all boards the same way and rely on a substrate or battens instead. Either way, the top must be allowed to move: elongated screw slots, buttons in grooves, or breadboard ends pinned only at the centre.

For frame-and-panel doors, use quartersawn or rift for the stiles and rails, since they must stay straight and hold the door square, and use whatever you like for the floating panel, which is free to move within its groove. Traditional joinery solved the movement problem structurally two centuries before anyone measured shrinkage coefficients.

For table and chair legs, riftsawn is the ideal, giving straight grain on all four faces and equal shrinkage. For chair spindles, ladder rungs, tool handles, axe hafts and anything loaded in bending, straight grain along the whole length matters far more than the cut category; riven stock is best, and if buying sawn, look for grain run-out of no more than about one in fifteen along the length.

For flooring, quartersawn or rift is markedly better: it wears more evenly because the dense latewood bands present their edges to the traffic rather than their faces, it cups far less under seasonal humidity swings and spills, and it opens narrower winter gaps between boards. It also costs more, and engineered flooring sidesteps the whole question with a cross-laminated core.

For exterior joinery — sash windows, doors, sills — vertical grain is the historic specification for good reason: it sheds water better because fewer ring boundaries are exposed on the surface, checks less under wetting and drying cycles, and holds paint longer, since paint films fail first over the wide flatsawn latewood bands that swell most. For musical instruments, quartered is close to universal for soundboards, since stiffness across the grain is highest on the quarter.

sections.heading: Drying and Seasoning: How the Cuts Behave in the Stack
sections.body:
How a board was cut changes how it should be dried, and drying is where most timber is ruined. Green wood leaves the saw somewhere between forty and two hundred percent moisture content depending on species and season. Air drying in a temperate climate brings it to an equilibrium in the region of twelve to eighteen percent, which is fine for exterior work and useless for interior furniture; heated interiors in winter drive wood down to six to eight percent, so interior stock must be kiln dried or brought indoors for months before use.

Quartersawn boards dry faster and more evenly than flatsawn ones of the same thickness, because the rays act as prepared pathways for moisture moving toward the face. They also degrade far less: they do not cup, they check less on the face, and their end checks tend to be fewer. Flatsawn boards dry with a strong tendency to cup toward the bark side and to develop surface checks along the wide, weak earlywood bands. The commonest single mistake in home air drying is drying too fast in the first weeks, when the surface loses moisture faster than the core can supply it, putting the shell into tension and opening checks that never close.

Good stacking practice is the same regardless of cut but matters most for flatsawn stock. Stickers — dry, uniform strips typically 19 to 25 millimetres thick — go between every layer, aligned vertically through the whole stack and spaced no more than about 400 millimetres apart, with a sticker flush at each end. Misaligned stickers produce a visible permanent bend at every unsupported point. The stack sits on a level, well-supported base at least 300 millimetres off the ground, is weighted on top with concrete blocks or steel, and is roofed but open at the sides. End grain is sealed within hours of sawing with wax emulsion, latex paint or proprietary end sealer, because moisture leaves end grain ten to fifteen times faster than face grain and unsealed ends check deeply.

The old rule of thumb is one year per inch of thickness for air drying hardwood in a temperate climate, which is roughly one year per 25 millimetres. It is a crude figure — thin softwood in a dry summer can be done in weeks, thick oak in a damp climate can take longer than the rule suggests — but it sets expectations correctly. Air drying alone will not reach interior equilibrium, will not kill insects, and will not relieve case hardening; a final kiln or at least several months in a heated space is needed for furniture stock.

Measure rather than guess. A resistance moisture meter with insulated pins costs little and is accurate enough between about seven and twenty-five percent; pinless capacitance meters read a shallow depth and are convenient for checking a finished board. For a definitive figure, cut a sample from at least 300 millimetres in from the end, weigh it, dry it at 103 degrees Celsius to constant mass, and compute the loss as a percentage of the dry mass.

sections.heading: Historical Practice and Regional Traditions
sections.body:
The three cuts are not modern inventions; they are names given to practices that long predate the vocabulary. Before powered saws, splitting was the default. Medieval European joinery in oak is overwhelmingly riven, because a froe and a beetle produce radial boards from a straight-grained log far faster than a pit saw does, and the results are stable and strong. Wainscot, the panelling of medieval and Tudor interiors, was radially cleft or radially sawn oak imported in quantity from the Baltic; the very word came to mean quartered oak panelling. That is why so much surviving sixteenth- and seventeenth-century oak furniture shows ray fleck and remains flat after four hundred years: it was not a stylistic choice so much as the natural output of the technology.

The industrial revolution inverted the default. Circular and band saws made it cheap to cut a log into parallel slices, and flatsawn lumber became the standard product because it maximised yield per minute of machine time. Quartersawing survived where performance justified the cost: barrel staves, which must be radial or the cask leaks through the rays; shipbuilding and boat decking; piano soundboards and violin bellies; and the vertical grain Douglas fir that floored a generation of North American houses.

The most visible historical revival came with the Arts and Crafts movement around the turn of the twentieth century. Gustav Stickley in New York, the Roycrofters, Charles Rennie Mackintosh in Glasgow and later Frank Lloyd Wright made quartersawn white oak into a design signature, often with ammonia fuming, which reacts with the oak's tannins to darken the wood while leaving the low-tannin ray flakes comparatively pale, exaggerating the fleck. That association is so strong that quartersawn oak still reads visually as period furniture to most viewers.

Regional vocabularies differ in ways that cause genuine confusion in trade. In Britain, through-and-through and slash-sawn describe what North Americans call live sawing; billet sawing, quarter sawing and rift sawing are used with specifications that vary between standards documents. In continental European practice the ring-angle bands are often stated in a standard rather than left as trade custom. Japanese woodworking distinguishes masame, the straight-grained quartered face, from itame, the flatsawn figured face, and applies them deliberately: masame for the visible faces of fine joinery and tansu, itame where figure is wanted. Scandinavian traditions rate slow-grown, tight-ringed, quarter-oriented pine so highly that old-growth reclaimed timber commands a premium precisely for its ring count.

Barrel-making deserves a final note because it is the purest demonstration of the principle. Wine and whisky casks are made only from quartered oak, historically riven, because a stave with rays running through its thickness lets liquid track along the ray tissue and weep.

sections.heading: Failure Modes and What to Do When It Goes Wrong
sections.body:
Most sawn-timber failures announce themselves in one of a handful of ways, and most are recoverable if diagnosed early. The commonest is a flatsawn panel that has cupped. If the cup is recent and the board has simply picked up moisture unevenly — typically because one face was exposed and the other was against a bench or wall — the cure is often to equalise the exposure: turn the board over, sticker it so air reaches both faces, and give it days to weeks. Wetting the concave face and weighting the board flat can work but frequently rebounds, because it treats the symptom. If the cup is permanent, the options are to plane it flat and accept the lost thickness, to rip the board into narrower strips and re-glue them with alternating orientation, or to constrain it mechanically with battens on slotted screws.

A tabletop that has split along a glue line, or across a breadboard end, is nearly always a restraint failure rather than a glue failure. Wood shrinking against a rigid fastener generates stresses that comfortably exceed its own tensile strength across the grain, which is only a few megapascals. The repair is to release the restraint — elongate the screw holes, unpin the outer breadboard pegs, replace fixed cleats with buttons — and then close the split with a bow-tie key, a glued spline or an epoxy fill. Re-gluing without releasing the restraint reproduces the failure in the next season.

Doors and drawers that bind only at certain times of year are a movement problem, not a fitting problem. A drawer front that sticks in August has swollen in width; plane the top edge, not the sides, and leave a seasonal clearance of about one millimetre per hundred millimetres of width for flatsawn stock in a swinging climate, less for quartered.

Tear-out when planing quartered flecked oak is a tool problem with a straightforward answer: reduce the effective cutting angle problem by increasing it. A high-angle plane, a back-bevelled blade taking the effective angle to fifty or fifty-five degrees, a tightly set chipbreaker within a fraction of a millimetre of the edge, or a card scraper will all cure it where a standard forty-five-degree bench plane tears.

Boards that twist as you machine them have internal stress, either from case hardening or from reaction wood. The practical response is to machine in stages: take material off both faces alternately rather than all from one, rough all parts oversize, let them sit for several days, then finish to dimension. If a board twists violently the moment it is ripped, it contains reaction wood and should be relegated to short parts, where the stress has too little length to act.

Finally, when a board is simply the wrong cut for the job, the honest answer is to use it elsewhere rather than fight it.

sections.heading: Buying, Specifying and Getting What You Paid For
sections.body:
Buying by category alone is a reliable way to be disappointed, because the words describe bands on a continuum and are applied loosely by honest sellers. The reliable approach is to specify what you actually need and then verify it in person or by photograph of the end grain.

When specifying, state the ring angle rather than the trade name where it matters: asking for oak with growth rings at sixty degrees or steeper to the face across the full width is unambiguous, where asking for quartersawn is not. State the minimum width you need after edging, because quartered boards are narrow and a supplier may otherwise send several narrow pieces. State whether you want fleck or specifically want it avoided, since that is the difference between quarter and rift in the oak trade and it is the most common source of a customer being sent the wrong thing. State a moisture content — six to eight percent for interior furniture in a heated climate, ten to twelve for exterior joinery — and be prepared to check it on arrival with a meter, because kiln-dried stock that has sat in an unheated shed for a winter is no longer kiln dried in any useful sense.

Sources worth knowing, roughly in order of price. Small local sawmills and portable-bandmill operators sell green or air-dried boules; buying a whole boule is the cheapest route to quartered stock, since the centre boards come free with the outers. Hardwood dealers sell graded, kiln-dried lumber and will usually let you sort, which is worth a long drive. Specialist suppliers for instrument makers, boatbuilders and turners sell small quantities of exactly specified riven and quartered stock at high prices. Reclaimed timber merchants sell old-growth material whose ring counts and stability are unobtainable new, though it must be metal-detected before it meets a blade. Firewood dealers and arborists occasionally have logs that a small mill will cut for a fee.

For grading, the North American hardwood system defined by the National Hardwood Lumber Association grades by the proportion of clear cuttings obtainable, with FAS at the top, then FAS one face, Selects, and the Common grades. That system says nothing at all about ring angle, so a top-grade board can be entirely flatsawn. Softwood grading in North America and the European strength-grading standards do address grain orientation, and vertical grain designations typically require forty-five degrees or steeper.

Finally, buy more than you need. A sensible allowance is twenty to thirty percent over the calculated net volume for defects, edging and the boards that turn out to be the wrong cut once you square an end and actually look at them.

guides.title: Buying Rough Lumber and Reading a Board
guides.summary: How rough-sawn lumber is produced, measured, graded, dried and priced, and how to read an individual board for grain, defects, distortion and internal stress before you buy it.

sections.heading: Why Rough Lumber Exists, and What You Gain by Buying It
sections.body: A board that comes off a sawmill has been cut to a nominal thickness and left with the saw's own marks on every face. It is not flat, its edges are not parallel, its thickness varies, and its width is whatever the log gave. This is rough lumber, and for most of the history of woodworking it was the only lumber there was. The alternative on offer at a home centre is surfaced lumber, usually described as S4S, meaning surfaced on four sides: planed smooth, ripped to a standard width, and sold at a fixed dimension. S4S is convenient and it is what most beginners start with, but it carries three quiet penalties. First, you pay for the material that was planed away and thrown out, because pricing is based on the size before surfacing. Second, the surfacing was done at the mill, often months ago and hundreds of miles away in a different climate, so the board has had ample time to move since; a piece that was dead flat when it was planed may arrive at your bench with a curve you now have no thickness left to remove. Third, the selection is narrow. A typical builders' merchant stocks softwood framing lumber, perhaps poplar and red oak, in widths up to 300 mm and one or two thicknesses. Rough lumber opens the whole species list, thicknesses up to 100 mm or more, widths limited only by the log, and prices that are commonly forty to sixty per cent lower per unit of usable wood. The trade is straightforward: you take on the milling yourself, and you take on the risk of judging the board. Both of those are learnable skills rather than mysteries, but they are real skills, and the second is the harder one. Milling is a mechanical process with a known sequence and a known outcome. Judging a board means predicting how a piece of once-living tissue, still exchanging water with the air around it, will behave over the next several years in a room you have not yet built it for. A woodworker who buys well wastes little; one who buys badly can lose half a stack to distortion that was visible in the yard if you knew where to look. The material is also finite in a way manufactured sheet goods are not. Wide clear boards come from large old trees, and a 400 mm wide clear walnut plank represents perhaps eighty years of growth that will not be repeated on the same land within your lifetime. Buying rough is partly an economic decision and partly an ethical one about using that material to its limit rather than discarding a third of it in shavings you never had to make.

sections.heading: How a Tree Becomes a Board: Log Geometry and Sawing Patterns
sections.body: Everything a board will later do is decided by where it sat in the log. A tree trunk is, structurally, a bundle of long hollow cells running vertically, laid down in annual increments outward from the centre. The centre itself is the pith, a soft core a few millimetres across that was the original shoot. Around it are growth rings, each one a year in temperate climates: a band of large thin-walled cells formed in spring, called earlywood, followed by a band of small thick-walled cells formed later in the season, called latewood. Latewood is darker and denser, and the contrast between the two is what you see as grain pattern. Radiating outward from the pith like the spokes of a wheel are rays, sheets of cells that move sap horizontally. In oak these rays are large enough to appear as bright flecks when cut a certain way; in maple they are fine; in most softwoods they are nearly invisible. Near the centre of an older tree the cells have stopped conducting water and have been infiltrated with extractives, chemicals that darken the wood and often make it decay-resistant. That is heartwood. The pale outer band still conducting sap is sapwood, typically 25 to 50 mm thick, less durable and in many species markedly less valuable. The sawyer's job is to decide how to slice this cylinder into rectangles. The commonest method is plain sawing, also called through-and-through or flat sawing: the log is squared and cut into parallel slabs like a loaf of bread. This is fast, wastes little, and yields the widest boards, but the ring orientation varies enormously across the stack. Boards cut near the outside of the log have rings running nearly parallel to the face; boards through the middle have rings crossing the face at right angles. Quarter sawing splits the log into quarters first and then cuts each quarter so the rings meet the face at between 60 and 90 degrees. It is slower, wastes more, and produces narrower boards, so quartersawn stock commonly costs 30 to 100 per cent more. Rift sawing aims for rings at roughly 30 to 60 degrees, produced either deliberately or as the by-product between quartered and flat cuts. In practice a single flitch from a plain-sawn log contains all three orientations, and one of the most useful skills at a lumber yard is looking at the end grain of a board and reconstructing in your head exactly where in the log it came from. That reconstruction tells you, before you have touched a tool, how the board will shrink, how it will cup, how it will take a finish, and how likely it is to still be flat next winter.

sections.heading: Board Feet, Nominal Dimensions and How Lumber Is Actually Priced
sections.body: Rough hardwood is sold by volume, not by length, and the standard unit in North America is the board foot: 144 cubic inches, equal to a piece 12 inches square and one inch thick, or about 2,360 cubic centimetres. The working formula is thickness in inches multiplied by width in inches multiplied by length in inches, all divided by 144. A board 1 inch thick, 8 inches wide and 96 inches long is therefore 1 times 8 times 96 divided by 144, which is 5.33 board feet. Many yards use a shortcut with length measured in feet: thickness times width times length-in-feet, divided by 12. Outside North America lumber is generally sold by the cubic metre; one cubic metre is about 424 board feet, so a price of four dollars per board foot corresponds to roughly 1,700 dollars per cubic metre. Rough thickness is quoted in quarters of an inch. Four-quarter, written 4/4 and spoken as four-quarter, is nominally one inch; 5/4 is one and a quarter; 8/4 is two inches; 12/4 is three. This scale survives because it describes the sawyer's setting, and because it makes the critical point that the number is a starting thickness, not a finished one. A 4/4 board typically finishes at 20 to 22 mm, about thirteen-sixteenths of an inch, after you have flattened both faces. If your design needs a full 25 mm you must buy 5/4.
