The mechanism is uneven absorbency: soft earlywood and random resinous patches drink deeply while dense latewood sips, sometimes even reversing the ring pattern into a photographic negative. The cures all work by throttling absorption. A washcoat, dewaxed shellac thinned to roughly a half-pound cut, or a commercial pre-stain conditioner, partially seals the thirsty zones so colour lands evenly; gel stains, whose thick body sits on the surface rather than soaking, achieve the same end from the other direction, and toned topcoats, colour carried in the film itself, sidestep absorption entirely. Always rehearse the full schedule, conditioner, stain, and topcoat, on offcuts from the actual boards, because pine lots vary wildly. Knots are the second ambush. A live knot is end grain saturated with resin, and both properties cause trouble: the resin dissolves into and yellows through paint, sometimes within months, and seasonal movement cracks coatings around the knot's rim. The traditional remedy survives because it works: seal every knot with shellac, either brush-applied knotting solution or a shellac-based stain-blocking primer over the whole surface, before painting. Kiln schedules that reach about seventy-one degrees Celsius set the resin, making factory-dried stock better behaved than air-dried, but sun on a dark-painted door can still liquefy pitch years later, so expect occasional weeping from resinous species and choose light colours for pine in hot exposures. Resin also interferes with curing: the aromatic oils in fresh cedar and the pitch streaks in pine can keep oil-based finishes tacky, another argument for shellac's universal sealing powers. Beyond the ambushes, softwood finishing follows its own physics. Because the wood is soft, film finishes flex and dent with it; a thick, brittle varnish on a pine table simply chips in white rings around every impact, so either accept a patina-friendly thin finish, oil, wax, or a wiping varnish, or commit to a tougher waterborne polyurethane and accept that dents will show through. Water-based finishes raise the grain sharply on soft species, so wet the surface, let it dry, and cut back the fuzz with fine paper before the first coat. Sanding grit changes colour uptake: surfaces sanded to very fine grits burnish and reject stain, so stop around 150 to 180 grit where stain is planned. End grain must be sealed or it will finish nearly black. Outdoors, remember that no clear film survives sun on softwood for long; ultraviolet destroys the wood surface under the film and the finish peels in sheets, so exterior softwood wants either paint over primer, a penetrating semi-transparent stain that fails gracefully by fading, or no finish at all, letting cedar, larch, or redwood weather to an even silver. Prime the back and edges of exterior boards, seal end cuts, and re-coat on a schedule rather than after failure.

sections.heading: When Softwood Goes Wrong: Warp, Rot, and Dust
sections.body: Most softwood failures are predictable, which means most are preventable, and the catalogue is short. Warp comes in four geometries, bow along the face, crook along the edge, cup across the width, and twist, and each has a mechanism. Cup is the two-to-one shrinkage difference between tangential and radial directions expressing itself in a flatsawn board; bow and crook come from drying gradients or from reaction wood sawn into one face; twist comes from spiral grain and from the juvenile core of fast-grown logs. Buy around warp by reading end grain, design around it by using narrower boards, quartersawn stock, and frame-and-panel construction, and correct mild cases by re-flattening after the wood has finished acclimatizing; twist, once established, rarely surrenders. Splitting is the second failure family. Wood is weakest in tension across the grain, so fasteners near ends, trapped cross-grain constructions, and rapid end-grain drying all open cracks; pilot holes, slotted fastenings, and end-grain sealant on fresh cuts are the standing defences. Brash failure, a sudden, carrot-like snap with no splintering, signals compression wood or early decay and disqualifies a board from anything structural, including ladder rails and chair legs. Rot is chemistry with a moisture switch. The fungi that digest wood need oxygen, mild temperatures, and sustained moisture above roughly twenty percent; keep softwood below that and it lasts indefinitely, as thousand-year-old roof timbers prove. Brown rots leave brittle, cubically cracked, crumbling wood, the classic building decay, including the misnamed dry rot fungus Serpula lacrymans, which conducts its own water through masonry to colonize dry timber; white rots bleach and soften; soft rots roughen saturated surfaces. Design, not chemistry, is the first defence: shed water with overhangs and drips, ventilate cavities, keep wood one hundred fifty millimetres clear of soil, and detail every horizontal surface to drain. Where wood must sit wet or in the ground, use pressure-treated stock, modern copper azole and alkaline copper quaternary having replaced the arsenic-bearing CCA now restricted in most consumer markets, and use borate treatments for indoor insect and rot protection. Handle treated offcuts with gloves and never burn them, because combustion concentrates the metals in ash and smoke. Insects, longhorn beetles, powderpost relatives, and termites, exploit the same negligence as fungi and yield to the same moisture discipline plus treatment where risk is high. The final hazard is the maker. Fine wood dust is a Group 1 human carcinogen by IARC classification, with nasal cancers documented in chronically exposed workers, and western red cedar dust carries plicatic acid, a sensitizer that gives a measurable fraction of exposed workers occupational asthma; its workplace exposure limit, at half a milligram per cubic metre, is the tightest of any wood. Collect dust at the machine, filter the room air, wear a fitted P100 or FFP3 respirator for sanding and cedar work, and manage finishing rags with equal respect, since linseed-oil-soaked cloth self-heats and ignites; dry rags flat or drown them in water. Softwood forgives almost everything else; it does not forgive being kept wet, stressed across the grain, or breathed.

guides.safetyNote: Wood dust is a recognized carcinogen and western red cedar dust is a potent respiratory sensitizer: extract dust at the machine and wear a well-fitted P100 or FFP3 respirator when sanding. Never burn or inhale sawdust from preservative-treated lumber, and wear eye and hearing protection whenever machines are running.

guides.title: Timber Defects: Knots, Shakes and Checks
guides.summary: How knots, shakes, checks and related timber defects form in the growing tree and during drying, how they affect strength and workability, and how to grade, select, work around, repair or reject defective wood.

sections.heading: Why Timber Defects Matter
sections.body: Timber is the only common structural material that is grown rather than manufactured, and every board carries within it the biography of the tree it came from. A steel beam rolled to a given specification is, within tight tolerances, identical to every other beam of that grade; a piece of wood is not. Branches, storms, drought, leaning growth, fungal attack and the stresses of drying all leave permanent marks in the material, and the three most consequential of those marks are knots, shakes and checks. A knot is the buried base of a branch. A shake is a separation along or between the growth rings that develops in the standing tree or at felling, before the wood is ever dried. A check is a crack that opens as the wood dries and shrinks. Understanding them matters for three distinct reasons. The first is safety: a single large knot on the tension edge of a floor joist can halve its bending strength, and timber grading rules exist almost entirely to police defects of this kind. Structural standards such as the American Softwood Lumber Standard PS 20 and the British visual grading standard BS 4978 are, at their core, systems for measuring knots and fissures and translating them into allowable working stresses. The second reason is economy. Sawmills lose a substantial fraction of every log to defect; clear, straight-grained material commands several times the price of knotty stock, and a furniture maker who cannot read a board in the timber yard will pay premium money for wood that ends up in the offcut bin. The third reason is craft. Defects govern how wood behaves under the tool. Grain rises and dives around a knot, so a hand plane that cuts cleanly along the clear length of a board will tear out savagely beside it, and a check hidden inside a turning blank can burst the piece apart on the lathe at speed, which is a genuine hazard to the person standing in front of it. None of this means defective wood is worthless. Carpenters have built sound roofs from knotty pine for centuries by placing the defects where stresses are low, and modern engineered products such as glued laminated beams and finger-jointed studs exist precisely to cut defects out and disperse what remains. Some defects are even prized: burr figure, the swirling grain around clusters of dormant buds, is among the most expensive wood sold, and knotty pine panelling is a deliberate aesthetic choice rather than an economy. The skill this guide aims to build is judgement, and judgement rests on mechanism. Once you understand how a branch becomes a knot, why a tree can tear itself apart from the inside, and why the outside of a drying board is stretched while the core is squeezed, you can predict where trouble will appear, decide what a given board is honestly fit for, and recognise the cases where the only correct decision is to reject a piece of timber entirely, however attractive its price or its figure.

sections.heading: How a Tree Grows: The Origin of Structure and Flaw
sections.body: Every property of timber, including its weaknesses, follows from the way a tree builds itself. Wood is laid down by the cambium, a sheath of dividing cells wrapping the trunk just beneath the bark. Each growing season the cambium adds a new cylinder of wood over the old, which in temperate climates appears in cross-section as an annual ring; count the rings and you have the age of the tree. Within each ring the cells formed in spring, the earlywood, are wide and thin-walled to conduct sap, while the latewood cells of summer are narrow and thick-walled, which is why latewood looks darker and denser and why fast-grown softwood with very wide rings is often weaker than slow-grown stock of the same species. The working cells themselves are essentially long hollow straws of cellulose bound together by a stiffening polymer called lignin, and they run overwhelmingly up and down the trunk. This is the fact from which nearly everything else follows: wood is anisotropic, meaning its properties differ enormously with direction. Along the grain the cellulose straws carry load magnificently; across the grain, load is carried only by the comparatively weak bonding between the straws, and strength in tension perpendicular to the grain can be a twentieth to a thirtieth of the strength along it. The trunk also contains rays, ribbons of storage tissue running radially from the centre toward the bark like the spokes of a wheel; they give quartersawn oak its silver figure, but they are also natural planes of weakness along which shakes and checks preferentially open. As the tree ages, the inner cylinder of wood retires from sap conduction and becomes heartwood, usually darker and richer in extractives that resist decay, while the outer working band remains as sapwood, which in nearly every species is perishable and attractive to insects. A living trunk is astonishingly wet: green wood commonly holds between 60 and 200 percent moisture content, expressed as the weight of water divided by the weight of oven-dry wood, and everything above roughly 30 percent must leave before the wood is dimensionally stable indoors. Finally, consider the branches. A branch does not sit on the surface of the trunk; it originates at or near the pith, the central core laid down in the first year of growth, and its base is buried a little deeper by every season of new wood the cambium sweeps over it. The mature trunk therefore contains, embedded in its clear outer cylinder, a set of branch bases reaching back like cones to the centre. Sawing does not create knots; it merely reveals this geometry. The first several rings around the pith, called juvenile wood, also have shorter cells, higher longitudinal shrinkage and lower strength than mature wood, so boards containing the pith misbehave in drying almost as reliably as boards containing knots. Read a log with this architecture in mind and its defects stop being random blemishes: they are the predictable consequences of a branching, layered, shrinking organism.

sections.heading: The Anatomy of a Knot
sections.body: A knot is the base of a branch entombed in the wood of the trunk. Because a branch begins life at or near the pith and thickens along with the trunk, its buried base is a cone whose tip lies near the centre of the tree and whose diameter grows outward year by year. What the sawyer's blade exposes depends entirely on where the cut passes through this cone, which is why the same knot can appear as a tidy circle on one face of a board and as a long oval or a dramatic spike on another. While the branch is alive the situation is structurally benign: the cambium of the trunk and the cambium of the branch are continuous, so each new growth ring flows without interruption from trunk into branch. Wood formed during this period grips the branch base completely, producing what is called an intergrown or live knot, usually darker and denser than the surrounding wood but anatomically continuous with it. When the branch dies, whether from shading in a crowded stand, storm damage or deliberate pruning, that continuity ends. The dead stub no longer grows, but the trunk keeps thickening around it, and each subsequent ring flows past the stub the way a river flows past a post. The new wood merely encases the branch base, often trapping a collar of bark around it, and the result is an encased or dead knot: a plug of branch wood held in place by geometry rather than by any living connection. Because the plug shrinks at different rates and in different directions from the wood surrounding it, drying frequently loosens it, and it may fall out entirely, leaving a knot hole. Eventually a healthy tree occludes the stub: the advancing growth rolls over the dead end, seals it, and every ring formed afterwards is clear, defect-free wood. This is why the outer boards of a large old-growth log can be flawless while its core is knotty, and it is why foresters prune plantation trees early, removing lower branches while they are still small so that only a slender defective core forms and decades of clear wood accumulate outside it. The knot itself is peculiar material. In softwoods it is commonly saturated with resin, which is why pine knots glow amber, weep sticky beads in warm sun and blunt edge tools quickly. Its grain runs at roughly a right angle to the face of the board, presenting hard end grain in the middle of a flat surface, and its density can be half again greater than that of the surrounding wood. Yet the most damaging feature is not the hard plug but the disturbance around it: the trunk fibres must sweep around the buried branch, so grain direction in the neighbouring wood deviates sharply for a distance comparable to the diameter of the knot itself. That swirl of short, crossed grain, not the knot proper, carries most of the mechanical penalty and most of the trouble under the plane.

sections.heading: Classifying Knots: Sound, Dead, Encased and Spike
sections.body: Craftspeople and grading rules slice the world of knots along three independent axes: condition, geometry and position. Condition asks how the knot is attached and what state it is in. A sound knot is solid, free of decay, and at least as hard as the surrounding wood; if it is also intergrown with the surrounding fibres for most of its circumference it is called a live or tight knot and will stay put indefinitely. A dead knot is one formed after the branch died; where the surrounding wood merely wraps it, graders call it encased, and the tell-tale sign is a dark ring of included bark around its rim. A loose knot is an encased knot that drying has already freed, rattling in its socket or ready to drop out, and a knot hole is the socket after the plug has gone. An unsound or rotten knot is one the fungus reached before the tree sealed the stub, and it warns of possible decay running deeper into the trunk. Geometry is set by how the saw crossed the buried branch cone. Cut the cone roughly square to its axis and you get a round knot; cut it obliquely and you get an oval; slice it nearly lengthwise and you get a spike or splay knot, a long triangular streak that can run across half the width of a board and is far more damaging than its area suggests, because the disturbed grain accompanies it along its whole length. Very small knots, conventionally those under about 6 millimetres across, are called pin knots and are often ignored by appearance grades or even prized, as in pippy oak. Knots may also come in clusters, several sharing one swirl of distorted grain where a whorl of branches grew at the same height, and a cluster is treated in grading as one large defect because the grain deviation is continuous across it. Position matters because bending members care intensely about where a defect sits. Grading language distinguishes face knots, appearing on the wide surface of a board, from edge knots on the narrow surface, arris knots that break the corner between the two, and margin knots that fall in the outer quarters of a beam's depth where bending stresses are highest. A modest knot centred on the neutral axis of a joist may be tolerable where the identical knot at the tension edge would condemn the piece. Grading rules therefore do not simply ask how big a knot is; they measure its projected size relative to the cross-section, note whether it occupies the margins, and cap both the size of any single knot and the total knottiness within any short length, since three medium knots clustered in 150 millimetres of joist are more dangerous than the same three spread over 2 metres. Learning this vocabulary is practical, not pedantic: it is the language in which every stamp, grade description and species datasheet communicates what the wood can be trusted to do.

sections.heading: How Knots Weaken Wood
sections.body: The mechanical damage a knot does comes from three stacked effects, and naming them explains almost every rule of thumb in the grading books. The first is simple loss of section: a dead or loose knot carries essentially no tensile load, so the effective cross-section of the board is reduced as though a hole had been drilled through it. The second is stress concentration. Load flowing through a plate must detour around a hole, and the stress at the edge of a circular hole in a uniform plate rises to roughly three times the average; a hard, poorly bonded inclusion behaves similarly. The third and largest effect is grain deviation. The fibres surrounding a knot swerve to flow around it, locally running 30 to 45 degrees or more off the axis of the board, and wood loaded at an angle to its grain is dramatically weaker: tensile strength perpendicular to the grain is commonly only 3 to 5 percent of strength parallel to it, so even partial cross-grain slashes capacity. Hankinson's formula, used by engineers since 1921, quantifies how strength falls as load rotates away from the grain direction, and it falls fast: at 45 degrees, many softwoods retain barely a fifth of their parallel strength. Put together, tests on structural lumber routinely show that a single knot occupying a third to a half of the depth of a joist can halve its bending strength, and knots are the governing defect in the majority of graded softwood. Where the knot sits changes everything. Wood fails in tension more brittly than in compression, so a knot in the tension zone of a bending member, the lower edge of a simple floor joist, is far more dangerous than the same knot in the compression zone above, and a knot at mid-depth, near the neutral axis where bending stress passes through zero, may cost little. This is why visual grading rules measure the knot area ratio, the fraction of the cross-section occupied by knots at the worst section, and separately a margin condition describing whether knots invade the outer quarters of the depth. Stiffness, interestingly, suffers much less than strength: a knotty joist deflects only somewhat more than a clear one, which is why a bouncy-but-intact floor tells you little about its reserve of strength, and why machine grading measures stiffness but calibrates it statistically against strength. Knots matter least in members loaded in pure compression over short lengths, since crushing is insensitive to local grain swirl, and they matter most in tension members such as the bottom chords of trusses, where codes are strictest. They also concentrate seasonal movement: the cross-grained halo shrinks differently from the straight wood around it, so paint cracks in rings around knots and joints loosen near them. The practical rules follow directly: keep big knots away from tension edges, never notch or bore near one, and judge a board by its worst 300 millimetres rather than its average character.

sections.heading: Working Wood That Contains Knots
sections.body: At the bench, a knot is less a strength problem than a workability problem, and the trouble begins with the plane. A hand plane cuts cleanly when the blade runs with the grain, lifting fibres that are supported by the fibres beneath; around a knot the grain reverses direction within a few centimetres, so whichever way you plane, part of the halo is being cut against the rise of the grain and tears out in divots. The remedies are the classic ones for any wild grain, applied with extra patience: a freshly sharpened blade, a very fine shaving, a tightly set chipbreaker within half a millimetre of the edge, a higher effective cutting angle of 55 to 60 degrees rather than the common 45, or abandoning the plane entirely for a card scraper or abrasives over the worst patch. The knot itself is end grain and often much harder than its surroundings, so it rounds over under sandpaper more slowly than the field around it; sand a knotty board carelessly with a soft backing pad and every knot ends up standing slightly proud, visible in raking light. Machine work has its own hazards. A knot entering a planer or circular saw presents a sudden change in density that can jolt the feed and chip brittle knot edges, and a loose knot can be flung by a cutterhead at considerable speed, one of several reasons eye protection at machines is not optional. Resinous softwood knots gum up blades and abrasive belts, and the resin problem follows the wood into finishing: pine knots continue to exude resin for years, especially when warmed above roughly 50 degrees Celsius by sunlight or a radiator, and the resin dissolves through most oil and water-based paints as a sticky amber bleed. The traditional cure, still the effective one, is to seal each knot before priming with two coats of knotting solution, which is shellac dissolved in alcohol; aluminium-flake primers also form an adequate barrier. Fastenings need forethought too. The dense knot resists nails and screws and will deflect a nail sideways, while the disturbed grain beside it splits far more easily than straight wood, so the working rule is to fasten either through sound straight grain well clear of the halo or, if a screw must land near a knot, to drill a full-diameter pilot hole. Loose and cracked knots can often be saved rather than cut out: thin cyanoacrylate glue wicked around a rattling pin knot fixes it permanently, and larger voids are filled with epoxy, tinted black or amber, a technique so reliable that knotty boards deliberately stabilised this way are now a mainstream furniture aesthetic. Joinery is the one place to be uncompromising. Never run a mortise, dovetail or tenon through a knot; the short cross grain leaves the joint with almost no strength, and the layout should shift or the board be re-crosscut so the joint lands in clear wood.

sections.heading: Shakes: Separations That Precede the Saw
sections.body: A shake is a lengthwise separation of the wood that exists before drying, and usually before felling: the tree itself has cracked from the inside. This distinguishes shakes from checks, which are made by the shrinkage of drying, and the distinction matters commercially because a shake reveals something about the whole log, not merely about one board's drying history. Shakes form because a standing trunk is not a calm object. It carries permanent built-in growth stresses, with the outer wood laid down in tension and the core consequently in compression, a prestressing arrangement that helps the stem resist wind but that stores energy like a spring; it is swayed and twisted through millions of wind cycles; it is frozen, thawed and heated unevenly; and at the end of its life it may be slammed to the ground over a stump or a rock. Any of these can start a separation along the planes where wood is weakest, either radially along the rays or circumferentially along the boundary between two growth rings, typically at the junction of dense latewood and the weak earlywood of the following spring. Certain circumstances make shake much more likely, and buyers of standing timber learn them as warning signs. Overmature and very large trees shake more than young ones. Open-grown trees exposed to wind, trees on shallow or waterlogged soils, and trees that have been struck by lightning or repeatedly stressed at one bend point are all suspect. In several species, notably oak, sweet chestnut, hemlock and true firs, ring shake is strongly associated with wetwood, heartwood infected by anaerobic bacteria that raise its moisture content and weaken the bond between rings; the wood often carries a sour smell and dries badly. The full causal story of ring shake remains genuinely unsettled, with researchers variously emphasising bacteria, frost, wind cycling and growth stress, and the honest summary is that these causes interact and that a shaken log rarely has a single culprit. What is not in doubt is the consequence. A shake is a pre-existing crack, indifferent to careful seasoning: no kiln schedule will close it, and drying usually extends it. In sawing, shakes waste wood wholesale, because the separation wanders through the log and every board it crosses either falls apart or must be docked short. In service, a shake parallel to the shear plane of a beam is particularly serious, since a beam carries load partly by horizontal shear along its length and a ring shake is a ready-made shear failure surface. Grading rules therefore treat through shakes harshly, limiting their length and forbidding them near bearings. At the yard, the place to look is the end grain: shakes show on the freshly crosscut end as curved or radial black lines, often stained by years of infiltrated water, while fresh drying splits look bright and clean.

sections.heading: Heart Shake, Star Shake, Ring Shake and Their Kin
sections.body: The traditional names for shakes describe their geometry as seen on the end of a log, and each pattern points to a different origin. A heart shake is a single radial split passing through or near the pith, widest at the centre and narrowing outward. It is characteristically a defect of overmature trees, where the oldest central wood has begun to weaken or decay, and it often accompanies incipient heart rot; a log with heart shake plus any discolouration around the pith deserves deep suspicion. A star shake is the plural case: several radial splits radiating from the centre like the points of a star, again widest at the heart. Severe star shake can result from growth stresses released at felling, from frost, or from the drying of the exposed log end, and it effectively quarters the core of the log before the sawyer gets a say. A ring shake, also called a cup or shell shake, follows the curve of a growth ring, separating one ring from the next along part or all of the circumference; a complete ring shake detaches a cylindrical shell, and a board sawn through it delaminates into two thin boards joined only at the edges. Ring shake is the form most strongly linked to bacterial wetwood and to species such as oak, chestnut and hemlock, and it is the most treacherous, because a partial ring shake can hide inside an apparently sound board and open only after machining. A frost crack or frost shake is a radial split that begins at the outside rather than the centre, caused by steep temperature gradients on bitter clear nights; the tree often heals it repeatedly, building a raised seam of callus bark called a frost rib down the trunk, and the healed crack with its included bark reappears inside the sawn wood. Related to shakes, though different in mechanism, are compression failures, known in the trade as thunder shakes or upsets: fine crinkled lines running across the grain rather than along it, produced when the wood fibres buckle in compression, either in the standing tree during storms or, very commonly, when a heavy tropical log is felled across a rock or another log. They are notorious in mahogany and other dense tropical timbers, are almost invisible on rough-sawn surfaces, and reduce the wood's bending strength catastrophically, since a board with a compression crease snaps across that line like a greenstick fracture, with a brash, carrot-like break instead of long splinters. Inspect any suspiciously cheap tropical hardwood in a raking light for faint dull lines across the planed face, and flex offcuts to destruction to see how the species should honestly break. As a class, shakes and compression failures teach the same lesson: some defects are inherited from the biography of the tree, cannot be dried out, planed out or glued shut economically, and must simply be found before the wood is trusted.

sections.heading: Checks and Splits: The Marks of Drying
sections.body: A check is a crack made by drying. As wood loses moisture it shrinks, and when the shrinkage of one part of a board is restrained by another part that has not yet shrunk, the wood tears along its weakest planes, which run along the grain and along the rays. The vocabulary is worth fixing precisely, because grading rules price these terms. A surface check is a shallow fissure opening on the face of a board, usually on the tangential face of flatsawn stock, following the grain for a few centimetres to a metre but penetrating only part way through the thickness. An end check appears on the end grain, and if a fissure passes right through from face to face it is called a split; a split at the end of a board, radiating from the end grain, is an end split, much the commonest of all. When a fissure passes through the board and extends in from the end it simply amputates usable length. Ends suffer first and worst for a mechanical reason with a memorable magnitude: water escapes along the open ends of the tubular wood cells far faster than it can diffuse sideways through cell walls, roughly ten to fifteen times faster, so the last few centimetres of a freshly cut board can drop below the fibre saturation point and begin shrinking within hours of crosscutting while the body of the board is still saturated. The wet interior refuses to shrink with the dry end, tension builds across the grain, and the end tears open along the rays. This is why every serious drying operation seals end grain within hours of cutting, traditionally with paraffin wax, thick paint or proprietary wax emulsion, and why boards in the yard are bought long, on the assumption that the last 50 to 150 millimetres of each end may be waste. Checks are not static. Wood keeps exchanging moisture with the air forever, swelling in humid summers and shrinking in heated winter interiors, so checks breathe: a hairline that is invisible in July can gape in January. A check that has opened and closed through seasons collects dirt and finish in its walls and will never close invisibly again. Structurally, surface checks in the faces of a joist are usually minor, because they run parallel to the bending stresses; codes begin to care when checks deepen toward the middle of the depth, where a beam carries its horizontal shear, since a deep check is partway to being a shear plane, and checks at bearing points or around bolted connections are treated more strictly still. In appearance work the tolerance is aesthetic and personal, but the mechanic's rule stands: measure depth with a feeler gauge, not by eye, because a modest-looking surface line can run surprisingly deep, and any check you can flex open with hand pressure has already found the thickness of the board.

sections.heading: Why Drying Cracks Wood: Shrinkage Mechanics
sections.body: The numbers that govern every check and warp are few enough to memorise. Water exists in green wood in two forms: free water filling the cell cavities like water in a straw, and bound water absorbed within the cell walls themselves. Drying removes the free water first, and this changes the weight of the wood but not its size. Only when the free water is gone, at what is called the fibre saturation point, roughly 28 to 30 percent moisture content for most species, does further drying begin to pull bound water out of the cell walls, and only then does the wood begin to shrink, stiffen and strengthen. Below the fibre saturation point, shrinkage is close to proportional to moisture loss, and its direction dependence is extreme. Longitudinally, along the grain, wood barely moves: about 0.1 to 0.3 percent from green to oven dry, which is why a dried plank keeps its length. Radially, across the rings, typical species shrink 3 to 6 percent. Tangentially, along the rings, they shrink 6 to 12 percent, roughly twice the radial figure. That two-to-one ratio between tangential and radial shrinkage is the single most consequential number in wood technology. It explains why flatsawn boards cup away from the heart, since their two faces contain different proportions of tangential direction; why square sections dry into diamonds; why a full round log, shrinking twice as much around its circumference as across its radius, must split radially because the circumference cannot get shorter without tearing; and why quartersawn boards, with rings running through the thickness, stay flatter and check less than flatsawn ones. Wood in service never stops moving, because it is hygroscopic: it continually adjusts toward an equilibrium moisture content set by the surrounding air, about 12 to 14 percent at 65 percent relative humidity and cool temperatures, falling to 6 to 8 percent in centrally heated winter rooms. A checking crisis is therefore always a gradient story. If the shell of a board dries below the fibre saturation point while the core is still above it, the shell tries to shrink around a core that has not budged; the shell goes into tension across the grain, and when that tension exceeds the modest perpendicular strength of the wood, a surface check opens. The steeper the moisture gradient, the greater the stress, which is why fast drying in hot sun or a fierce kiln checks wood that would have survived a gentle regime, why thick stock is at far greater risk than thin, and why dense hardwoods, which move more and pass moisture more slowly, demand the gentlest schedules of all. The rule of thumb for air drying, one year of seasoning per inch of thickness, is not folklore but a rough encoding of exactly this diffusion problem, and oak, the classic slow case, rewards even more patience.

sections.heading: Case-Hardening, Honeycomb and Hidden Stress
sections.body: Not all drying damage is visible on the surface; some of it is locked inside the board as stress, waiting for a saw to release it. The mechanism is called drying set. When the shell of a board dries first and is stretched in tension over a wet, unshrunk core, one of two things happens: either it checks, or it survives the tension by creeping, taking on a permanent stretch, like a wool jumper pulled while damp. A shell that has taken tension set is now permanently slightly too large for the core it encloses. As drying proceeds and the core finally dries and tries to shrink, the oversized shell will not let it, so the stresses reverse: the core ends up in tension and the shell in compression. Such a board is described as casehardened, a slightly misleading term borrowed from metallurgy, since the case is not hard, merely stressed. A casehardened board can look perfect, measure a uniform moisture content, and still be a trap: rip it down the middle and the two halves spring inward, pinching the saw blade, a genuinely dangerous event on a table saw; plane one face and the board cups as the balanced stresses are unbalanced; machine a deep groove and the walls close on the cutter. The standard test is simple and worth doing on any suspect kiln-dried stock: crosscut a slice about 25 millimetres thick from the middle of a board, bandsaw it into a comb of prongs, and watch. If the prongs stay parallel the board is stress free; if they curve inward and pinch together, it is casehardened; prongs curving outward indicate the rarer reverse condition. Commercial kilns fix casehardening at the end of the schedule by conditioning: a deliberate spell of high humidity, often with live steam, that re-wets the shell slightly and relieves the set. If the shell tension set is severe and the core, still wet, is then dried too hard, the core itself can fail internally in tension, tearing along the rays in hidden slit-like voids. This is honeycomb, the worst drying defect, invisible until a saw or a moulder opens the board and reveals an interior like torn paper; it cannot be repaired, and thick oak dried in a hurry is its classic victim. The practical defences follow from the mechanism. Dry gently through the danger zone above the fibre saturation point, protect end grain, and keep thick stock out of aggressive kilns; when buying, prong-test a sample from any pallet of kiln-dried hardwood, and be suspicious of thick stock offered dry at improbable speed or price. When resawing any thick dried board into thinner leaves, expect movement, take equal amounts from both faces where possible, cut oversize, and let the halves settle for days and re-equilibrate before final machining, because even well-dried wood retains modest stress and fresh surfaces hold different moisture than the old ones.

sections.heading: Wane, Reaction Wood, Pitch Pockets and Warp
sections.body: Beyond the big three, a family of lesser defects appears constantly in the yard and deserves quick, confident recognition. Wane is the simplest: the presence of the original rounded surface of the log, with or without bark, along an edge of a board, because the sawyer cut too close to the outside. It costs bearing area and nailing edge rather than strength within the remaining wood, and grading rules cap how much of an edge may be waney; in rustic furniture the same feature is sold, at a premium, as a live edge. Pitch pockets are lens-shaped voids between growth rings filled with liquid or crystallised resin, common in spruce, pine and Douglas fir, usually the scar of cambium damage or wind flexing; small ones are cosmetic, but a deep pocket weeps resin through finishes for years and a row of them hints at a wind-shaken tree. Bark pockets are the equivalent with included bark. More consequential is reaction wood, the abnormal tissue a leaning tree builds to right itself, in two opposite forms. Conifers build compression wood on the underside of a lean: wide-ringed, dull, lifeless-looking wood, often forming an off-centre pith, that is brittle, weak for its weight, and above all shrinks along the grain up to ten or twenty times more than normal wood. Because normal longitudinal shrinkage is nearly zero, a board with a streak of compression wood on one edge bows and springs violently as it dries and can keep moving for years; it also breaks suddenly across the grain, which is why grading rules for ladder stock and scaffold planks specifically exclude it. Hardwoods do the opposite, building tension wood on the upper side of the lean; it is gelatinous in texture, planes and sands to a woolly, fuzzy surface that will not take a crisp finish, and likewise shows abnormal longitudinal shrinkage. Both forms betray themselves by an off-centre pith on the end grain and by rings markedly wider on one side than the other. Finally there is warp, the umbrella term for shape error, with four named components that can occur separately or together. Bow is curvature along the length seen from the side; spring or crook is curvature along the length seen from the face, the enemy of straight edges; cup is curvature across the width, the natural fate of flatsawn boards drying with the two-to-one tangential-to-radial shrinkage ratio; and twist is the propeller condition, where the four corners will not sit in one plane, commonly born of spiral grain in the tree. Small amounts of bow and spring are removed by jointing at the cost of thickness and width; cup is flattened by ripping wide boards into narrower ones before jointing; but twist wastes more wood than any other warp, and a badly twisted or sprung board is usually best crosscut into short lengths, within which the error becomes trivial.

sections.heading: Biological Defects: Fungi and Insects
sections.body: Two thresholds organise everything about decay. Wood-destroying fungi need moisture and cannot attack wood kept below about 20 percent moisture content, a figure comfortably above the 8 to 14 percent of any heated or ventilated interior; and they need oxygen, which is why wood permanently submerged, like foundation piles under the water table, lasts for centuries. Decay is therefore not a property of old wood but of wet wood, and every rotten sill, joist end or fence post is a moisture problem before it is a fungus problem. The attack comes in recognisable forms. Brown rots consume the cellulose and leave the brown lignin skeleton, shrinking the wood into the characteristic cubical cracked pattern of dry rot and quickly destroying strength; the name dry rot for Serpula lacrymans is a misnomer worth correcting, since the fungus needs moisture to start, though it can then conduct water through its own strands to colonise adjacent dry wood, which is what makes it uniquely dangerous in buildings. White rots consume lignin and cellulose together, leaving pale, stringy, spongy wood, and are commoner in hardwoods. Soft rot roughens chronically wet surfaces like cooling towers and ground-line posts. Critically, strength is lost before decay is clearly visible: wood in the early, incipient stage, called dote or doze, can have lost a third or more of its toughness while showing only faint discolouration. The field test is the pick test: pry up a splinter with an awl; sound wood breaks out in a long fibrous splinter, decayed wood breaks brashly, straight across, with little resistance. Not all fungal marks matter equally. Blue stain or sap stain, a blue-grey discolouration of softwood sapwood, is a pigmented mould living on cell contents, not cell walls; it costs appearance grade but essentially no strength, and the related black-line spalting prized by woodturners is partial decay caught, ideally, before softening. Insects divide by habitat. Powderpost beetles of the Lyctus group attack only the sapwood of coarse-pored hardwoods such as oak and ash, packing tunnels with flour-fine dust; the common furniture beetle, the woodworm of old pine furniture, leaves 1.5 to 2 millimetre exit holes and gritty pellets; the house longhorn beetle mines softwood roof timbers and can be structurally devastating; termites, where they occur, consume wood from within, leaving a painted shell, and warrant professional attention rather than improvisation. Two field rules keep buyers out of most trouble. First, fresh activity shows as clean, pale exit holes and new dust; old, dark, empty holes in bone-dry wood are usually history, since most borers need the higher moisture of unseasoned or damp wood, though Lyctus and furniture beetle can reinfest dry sapwood. Second, sapwood is the vulnerable band in nearly every species: a board of durable heartwood with a strip of sapwood along one edge is durable except exactly there, and outdoors that strip should be cut off or treated, not hoped over.

sections.heading: Grading: How Defects Are Measured and Priced
sections.body: Grading is the institutional machinery that turns a visual inspection of defects into a number an engineer or buyer can use, and it comes in two great families. Appearance grading, used for hardwoods destined for furniture and joinery, asks how much clear, defect-free wood can be cut from a board. The rules of the National Hardwood Lumber Association, which govern the North American trade and influence practice worldwide, define the top grade FAS, historically Firsts and Seconds, essentially as boards of a minimum size yielding at least 83 and one third percent clear cuttings of specified sizes; the successive grades, Select, Number 1 Common, Number 2 Common and below, admit smaller and fewer clear cuttings, roughly two thirds for Number 1 Common. The crucial insight for a buyer is that a lower grade is not worse wood but smaller patches of the same clear wood interrupted by more defects; a maker of small components can often buy Number 1 Common at a large discount and cut around the knots to obtain identical material to FAS. Structural grading, used for softwood construction timber, instead asks how much strength the defects have removed from the piece as a whole. Visual structural grading, under standards such as BS 4978 in Britain or the National Grading Rule species rules in North America, has a trained grader assess each piece in seconds: knot sizes are measured by projection and expressed as a knot area ratio, the fraction of the cross-section occupied by knots at the worst point; a margin condition records whether more than half of the outer quarters of the section is occupied; slope of grain is limited, commonly to about 1 in 6 for lower grades and 1 in 10 or better for higher ones; and fissures, wane, distortion, resin pockets and decay each have caps. The piece is then stamped, for example GS or SS in the British system, and those visual grades map to strength classes, C16 or C24 for typical European softwood, whose design stresses engineers take from tables. Because visual grading must assume the worst about what it cannot see, it is conservative, and machine strength grading has largely supplemented it for high volumes: a machine flexes each board or measures its acoustic stiffness, exploiting the strong statistical correlation between stiffness and strength, and stamps a class accordingly, catching good-but-knotty and poor-but-clear pieces that fool the eye. Three practical warnings complete the picture. A grade stamp applies to the whole piece as graded; crosscutting can upgrade it, but ripping a graded joist into two thinner ones voids the stamp, since the defect geometry changes. Grade describes the piece at grading, not after decades of wetting. And grading is statistical: design stresses are set low enough that the fifth-percentile piece is safe, which is why regraded, reclaimed or ungraded timber in structural positions requires either an engineer's judgement or generous, honest oversizing.

sections.heading: Reading a Board: Selection and Cutting Strategy
sections.body: Everything above condenses, at the timber rack, into a five-minute inspection routine that repays itself on every purchase. Start at the ends, because the end grain is the board's confession. Ring curvature tells you whether the piece is flatsawn, with rings running roughly parallel to the wide face and maximum movement across the width, or quartersawn, with rings standing upright and half the movement; the position of the heart, if present, predicts cupping and juvenile-wood misbehaviour; dark curved or radial lines warn of shake; and end splits show you immediately how much length to write off. Next sight along both edges from one end, like sighting a rifle, which reveals bow, spring and twist far better than any straightedge laid flat; reject or heavily discount twist. Scan the faces for knots and classify them as you look: tight, intergrown knots that will stay put, or encased knots ringed with bark and loose plugs that will not, and note whether any spike knots run into the edges. Look for the dull, lifeless stripe of compression wood in softwood, for woolly patches in hardwood that betray tension wood, for pitch pockets, wane, insect holes and the grey of sapwood in a species where sapwood matters. Check moisture if anything structural or fine depends on it: a resistance meter pushed into the face should read within a few points of the equilibrium value for the wood's destination, roughly 8 to 10 percent for centrally heated interiors, 12 to 16 for outdoors under cover, and readings that differ sharply between shell and core, if the meter has insulated pins, warn of a wet centre or locked-in stress. Then buy deliberately more than the cutting list demands; experienced makers allow 20 to 30 percent extra for clear work in knotty species, more in low grades, because defect waste is a certainty, not a risk. The cutting strategy that follows is the craft of getting high-grade results from mid-grade wood. Crosscut first, freeing the cutting-list lengths from around the defects rather than ripping full length and hoping; dock end splits generously, cutting 50 millimetres beyond the visible end of the crack, because checks run further than they show. Place what remains: knots into internal, hidden or low-stress components, never into joints; the straightest, most vertical grain into legs, rails and anything that must stay straight; pith and juvenile wood into nothing that matters. For structural work the same logic becomes rule rather than art: bearing ends must be free of wane and rot, notches and bored holes must avoid knots and stay out of the tension edge, and a joist with a large edge knot can often simply be turned so the knot sits in the compression zone or crowned so its camber works with the load. Reading wood this way is not lore; it is applied mechanism, and after a few hundred boards it becomes as fast as looking.

sections.heading: Prevention, Repair and Knowing When to Reject
sections.body: Defect management begins the day the tree is felled. Logs left in the sun split from the ends within days, so mills seal log ends with wax emulsion and convert quickly; the same wax, or thick paint in an emergency, belongs on the end grain of every freshly sawn board within hours of cutting. Air drying is a discipline of geometry: boards stacked flat on level bearers, separated by uniform stickers of dry wood about 20 to 25 millimetres square placed in vertical lines every 400 to 600 millimetres, the whole pile roofed against sun and rain, its top weighted so the upper boards cannot warp, and the ends of the pile shaded, since sun on end grain is the great splitter. The classical pace is a year of air drying per inch of thickness down to outdoor equilibrium, followed, for furniture stock, by weeks of acclimatisation indoors or a gentle kiln finish to interior moisture levels; hurrying past either stage is how checks and casehardening are bought. In service, prevention is mostly moisture management: keep structural timber below 20 percent by ventilation and detailing so decay never starts, prime the end grain of every exterior component, and expect and design for seasonal movement rather than fighting it, which is the entire logic of frame-and-panel construction. When defects have already happened, repair is often honest and durable. A check or split that has stopped moving can be stabilised with a butterfly key, the bowtie-shaped inlay of contrasting hardwood set across the crack that Japanese and studio furniture makers have made a signature; cut the recess so the key's grain runs across the split and it mechanically stitches the two sides together. Epoxy resin, tinted or filled, consolidates checks and knot holes in tabletops and turnery; thin cyanoacrylate locks small loose knots; and a knot in painted joinery can be bored out entirely and replaced with a glued cross-grain plug. What repair cannot honestly do is restore strength across a structural fracture: a filled check is cosmetic, and a beam that has split at a bearing or sheared along a shake needs sistering, replacement or an engineer, not adhesive. Finally, the reject list, the cases where the correct decision is to walk away or saw the piece into firewood lengths regardless of price. Reject for structural use: ring shake anywhere, compression failures across the grain, active decay or any wood that fails the splinter pick test, large knots or knot clusters at the tension edge that exceed the relevant grade, and casehardened stock destined for ripping. Reject for fine work: twist beyond what thicknessing can afford, compression wood, honeycomb, and boards whose defects sit exactly where the design needs its joints. A defective board is only a bargain when its defects fall where the work does not; the whole craft of this subject is knowing, before money changes hands, whether they do.

guides.safetyNote: Never machine, rip or turn timber containing loose knots, ring shake, deep checks or suspected internal splits at full speed: pieces can detach or the stock can burst apart. Inspect both faces and both ends first, tap turning blanks for dead sounds, wear eye and face protection at machines, and reject decayed or shake-ridden wood for any load-bearing use.

guides.title: Reading Wood Grain, Figure and Runout
guides.summary: How to read a board: the cell structure behind grain, what growth rings and rays reveal, how to identify figure, and how to spot runout and grain direction so that wood is cut, planed, bent and joined with its structure rather than against it.

sections.heading: Why Reading a Board Is the First Skill
sections.body: Wood is the only common structural material that arrives already organised. Steel is isotropic, meaning it behaves the same in every direction, and a woodworker coming from metal or plastic has to unlearn that assumption completely. A piece of timber is a bundle of long hollow cells glued together, laid down by a tree that was solving its own problems: standing up, carrying water from root to leaf, and resisting wind. Every property that matters in the workshop follows from that arrangement. Timber is roughly twenty to forty times stronger in tension along the fibres than across them, splits readily in one plane and hardly at all in another, moves a great deal in width and almost not at all in length as humidity changes, and cuts cleanly in one direction while tearing in the other. Reading a board means inferring that internal arrangement from what is visible on its faces and ends, and then making every subsequent decision, which face to plane first, which way to feed it, where a joint can go, whether it will do as a chair leg, in accordance with what is actually inside it. Nearly all the frustrations that drive beginners to blame their tools are misreadings. A plane that tears out chunks on one pass and leaves glass on the reverse pass is not blunt; it was being pushed against the fibres. A door that binds every winter was made from flat-sawn stock that moves twice as much as quartersawn would have. A chisel handle that snapped near the ferrule almost certainly had grain running out of its side. There is also an economic argument. Timber varies enormously in price by grade and figure, and grading rules are largely descriptions of grain features. Being able to look at a rough board in a yard and see where the clear cuttings are, whether the apparent flaw is a knot cluster or harmless bark inclusion, whether the shimmer on the face is genuine curl or just a planing artefact, is the difference between buying wood well and buying it badly. Rough-sawn stock hides most of this under saw marks and dirt, and a block plane or a wetted thumb applied to a small patch will usually reveal enough. The vocabulary is unfortunately loose. Grain is used by different trades to mean the direction of the fibres, the size of the pores, the pattern on a face, and the general texture, and figure is often used interchangeably with it. Precision helps: grain direction is where the fibres point in three dimensions; grain pattern or ring pattern is what the growth rings draw on a surface; texture is the size and uniformity of the cells; and figure is any distinctive optical or structural pattern beyond the plain ring layout. Almost every confusing piece of woodworking advice becomes clear once these four are kept apart.

sections.heading: Inside the Tree: Cells, Rings, Rays and Sap
sections.body: A tree grows outward from a thin sleeve of dividing cells called the cambium, which lies immediately under the bark. Each season the cambium lays down new wood, xylem, on its inner face and new bark, phloem, on its outer face. That is why a nail driven into a trunk stays at the same height for a century while the trunk thickens around it, and why removing a ring of bark all the way round kills the tree. In temperate climates growth is seasonal, and the wood laid down in spring differs from that laid down in summer. Earlywood, formed during the rush of spring growth, has large thin-walled cells built for conducting water; latewood, formed later, has smaller thick-walled cells and is denser and darker. The alternation produces annual growth rings. In tropical species with no marked dry season, rings may be faint or absent entirely, which is one reason mahogany and many tropical timbers look so uniform. Counting rings gives age, and the discipline of dendrochronology, founded by A. E. Douglass in the early twentieth century, uses the varying widths of those rings to date timbers to the exact year and to reconstruct past climate; a Bronze Age log and a modern tree from the same region can be cross-matched on ring-width patterns alone. Running at right angles to the rings, radiating from the centre like spokes, are the rays: ribbons of cells that store food and move it sideways. In most species they are microscopic. In oak they can be a centimetre or more deep, and it is these that produce the silver flecks or medullary figure prized in quartersawn oak furniture. Rays are also planes of weakness, which is why oak splits so cleanly along a radius and why radial checks in a drying log always open along a ray. Two zones make up the cross-section of most mature trunks. Sapwood, the outer band, is living, conducts water, is usually paler, and contains starches that insects and fungi eat readily. Heartwood, the inner core, is dead conducting tissue that the tree has plugged and impregnated with extractives, the compounds that give teak, cedar, black walnut and yew their colour, smell and natural decay resistance. The practical consequences are direct: sapwood is not durable outdoors regardless of species, so a fence post of untreated pine sapwood may fail in three years where the heartwood of the same log lasts fifteen, and the pale stripe on the edge of a walnut board is not a defect of colour only but a genuinely different material. Hardwood and softwood, finally, are botanical labels, not measures of hardness. Hardwoods are broadleaved flowering trees with vessels, or pores; softwoods are conifers without them. Balsa is a hardwood and yew is a softwood, and both facts embarrass the terminology annually.

sections.heading: Sawing Patterns: Flat-Sawn, Quartersawn and Rift
sections.body: A log is round and boards are flat, so every board is a compromise, and which compromise was chosen determines how the board looks, how it moves and how much it cost. The controlling variable is the angle between the growth rings and the wide face of the board, read off the end grain. Flat-sawn, also called plain-sawn or through-and-through, means the rings meet the face at less than about thirty degrees, and in the boards nearest the centre of the log they run almost parallel to it. This is the cheapest conversion because the log is simply sliced straight through with minimal handling and almost no waste. It produces the familiar cathedral or flame pattern, nested arches on the face, formed where the plane of the cut slices obliquely through the cone-shaped ring surfaces. Flat-sawn stock is also the least stable: it moves roughly twice as much in width as quartersawn, and because the rings try to straighten as they dry it cups away from the heart, so the face that was nearer the bark becomes concave. Quartersawn means the rings meet the face at sixty to ninety degrees, standing nearly on edge. The log is quartered first and each quarter sawn radially, which costs far more in labour and yields narrower boards with more waste. The face shows straight parallel lines rather than arches, and in ray-rich species such as oak, plane, beech and lacewood, the cut slices along the ray plane and produces flecks, sometimes covering the whole surface. Quartersawn boards move about half as much across their width, do not cup, wear more evenly on a floor, and take finish more uniformly. Their historical association with Arts and Crafts and Mission furniture is not just taste; Gustav Stickley's oak was quartersawn because it stayed flat. Rift-sawn sits between, at roughly thirty to sixty degrees, and is usually specified to get the straight line pattern without the ray fleck, which is why rift white oak is standard for table legs where four faces should match. The numbers are worth carrying. For a typical hardwood moving between about seven and twelve per cent moisture content, tangential shrinkage runs around eight per cent of dimension, radial about four, and longitudinal about one tenth of one per cent. A 300 mm wide flat-sawn oak panel can therefore change width by five or six millimetres between a damp summer and a heated winter, while its length changes by a fraction of a millimetre. Every frame and panel door, breadboard end and buttoned tabletop in the history of furniture exists to accommodate that single asymmetry. Reading which conversion you have takes two seconds: look at the end grain and judge the ring angle, and if the rings arch across the end like a rainbow the board will cup away from that arch as it dries.

sections.heading: Grain Direction in Three Dimensions
sections.body: The single most useful mental model is to picture a board as a bundle of drinking straws glued side by side, then to accept that the bundle is almost never perfectly parallel to the board's edges. Grain direction is a three-dimensional fact and has to be read on more than one surface. On the end grain you see the straws in cross-section, and this tells you the sawing pattern and how the board will move. On the face and edges you see them in length, and this tells you which way to cut, plane and feed. The critical thing the face reveals is slope of grain: the angle between the fibres and the long axis of the board. A board sawn from a straight, vertically grown log has fibres nearly parallel to its edges. A board sawn from a leaning tree, a tapering butt log, or one sawn to a line that was not parallel to the pith, has fibres that run diagonally, and where a fibre reaches the surface and stops, that is runout. Slope of grain is measured as a ratio and it is worth learning to express it that way, because every strength rule uses it. If the fibres deviate by 25 mm over 300 mm of length, that is a slope of 1 in 12. Structural grading rules typically demand 1 in 10 or better for general framing, 1 in 12 to 1 in 15 for higher grades, and traditional practice for tool handles and ladder rails is 1 in 15 or straighter. Strength falls off far faster than intuition suggests: an approximation known as the Hankinson formula predicts that tensile strength at 1 in 10 is already down to roughly half the straight-grained value, and at 1 in 5 to something like a quarter, because the load starts being carried by the weak glue between fibres rather than by the fibres themselves. Reading direction on a planed face is a learned trick with three reliable methods. First, look at the edge of the board rather than the face: on a quartersawn or rift edge the fibre lines emerge at a shallow angle, and they point the way a plane should travel, uphill in the sense that you cut with the lie of the fibres rather than lifting them. Second, run a thumbnail or fingertip lightly along the surface in both directions; one direction feels smooth and the other slightly rough, and the smooth one is with the grain. Third, take a light test cut with a sharp plane at each end; the direction that leaves a shaving and a bright surface is right, the one that tears fibres out is wrong. For flat-sawn faces the cathedral arches give a further clue. The arches point like nested arrowheads, and planing in the direction the arches point, from the open ends of the arches toward their peaks, is usually correct. It is genuinely only a rule of thumb, because the arch pattern is a section through a cone and the fibre direction underneath does not always agree with it.

sections.heading: Runout: What It Is, How To See It, Why It Breaks Things
sections.body: Runout is the condition where fibres that were continuous inside the tree have been severed by the saw and now run out of the face or edge of a board. Look closely at any sawn face and you will see fibres that begin somewhere in the middle of it, taper and disappear: each of those is a fibre that was cut across rather than followed. Runout is not damage and not a defect of the tree. It is a consequence of making a straight cut through a material whose fibres were not straight. It matters because wood carries load along its fibres and hardly at all between them. The lignin and hemicellulose that bond adjacent cells are perhaps a twentieth as strong in tension as the cellulose chains running along them. A piece with continuous fibres from end to end behaves like a rope. A piece with severe runout behaves like a rope that has been cut most of the way through at an angle, and it will fail along the interface without warning at a fraction of the expected load. This is why a shop-bought hammer handle can snap in a season while a riven ash handle lasts three generations, and why the failure of a runout-crossed handle is sudden rather than gradual. Seeing runout takes practice but is not subtle once the eye has it. On a planed surface, look along the board at a low angle with a light source behind the far end; runout shows as fine hairlines or as short fibre ends catching the light. Bending the piece slightly and watching where the surface fibres tent up reveals it as well. The most reliable test is destructive and therefore reserved for offcuts: split a short sample with a froe or a chisel and see whether the split runs out to the side within a few centimetres. A split follows the fibres exactly, which is precisely what makes it a perfect indicator and also the reason riving exists. The strength requirement is only one half. The other is surface quality: runout is the direct cause of tearout in planing, because a blade meeting fibres that rise toward the surface lifts and levers them out ahead of the cut rather than severing them. It also causes ragged results in routing, ragged edges on sawn cuts, and blotchy stain because severed fibre ends absorb more finish than intact ones. The remedies form a hierarchy. Choose stock without severe runout for anything load-bearing, and reject rather than repair. Where runout is present and unavoidable, orient it so that it lies on a face in compression rather than tension, since compression across the fibre interface is far less dangerous. Reduce cutting angle problems with a high-angle or back-bevelled plane iron, a tight chipbreaker set a few tenths of a millimetre from the edge, or a scraper. And for handles, rungs, wedges, shingles and basket splints, do not saw at all: split the stock and let the wood choose the surface.

sections.heading: Riving and Splitting: Letting the Fibres Choose
sections.body: Riving is the deliberate splitting of green wood along its natural fibre planes, and it is the oldest conversion method there is, predating the saw by millennia. Its whole logic is that a split cannot cross fibres, so every riven surface is by definition a zero-runout surface. A riven billet has fibres continuous end to end even if the tree twisted, which is why handle, ladder, chair and basket makers all rive rather than saw. Green wood is very much easier to split than dry, typically requiring a third to a half the force, because the water plasticises the lignin and the fibres part rather than tearing. Ring-porous hardwoods split best: oak, ash, chestnut, hickory and hazel are the classic riving timbers. Interlocked-grain species such as elm barely split at all, which is why elm was chosen for wheel hubs and chair seats. The key technique is control of the split's path. A split naturally follows the thicker of the two sides, so it wanders toward the weaker half and can run off the end of a billet, wasting it. The fix is counter-intuitive: bend the thicker side. Levering the heavier half away from the split forces the crack back toward the middle, and that single manoeuvre is the whole craft of accurate riving. Because riven material works best green, the sequence is rive, shape wet with a drawknife, then season before final fitting.
ingredients: A straight, knot-free green log or bolt felled within a few weeks; oak, ash, sweet chestnut, hickory or hazel split most predictably.
A froe: an L-shaped blade 200 to 300 mm long with a handle at right angles, used as a steerable wedge rather than a cutting tool.
A club or maul of green wood, not a steel hammer, which would mushroom the froe's back.
Two or three steel or wooden wedges for starting splits in larger rounds.
A riving brake: two forked stakes that grip the billet and leave both hands free to lever.
A drawknife and a shaving horse for shaping the blank while it is still green.
steps: Cut the log to length with 50 to 100 mm of waste at each end, and reject any bolt showing spiral grain or knots within that length.
Stand the round on a solid block and start a split across the full diameter with a wedge and maul until it opens into halves.
Halve each half again, always into two equal parts rather than shaving off a slice; splitting off-centre almost always runs out.
At arm thickness switch to the froe: set the blade across the end grain, strike until it bites 30 mm, then stop hitting it.
Lever the handle sideways to propagate the split by wedging, walking the froe down into the crack as it opens.
The moment the split favours one side, hold the thicker half and bend it away; the crack steers back toward the centre.
Shape green and slightly oversize, then sticker the parts with 20 mm air gaps in shade for about a year per 25 mm of thickness.

sections.heading: Figure: What Makes a Board Beautiful
sections.body: Figure is any distinctive pattern on a wood surface beyond the plain layout of growth rings, and almost all of it is optical rather than pigmentary. The underlying physics is straightforward. Wood fibres act like bundles of tiny optical fibres; where they are cut at an angle, their exposed ends reflect light back toward a viewer differently from fibres lying flat. When the fibre direction undulates, some regions present ends and some present sides, and the pattern of light and dark reverses as the viewer or the light moves. That shifting, three-dimensional shimmer is called chatoyance, from the French for cat's eye, and it is the reason a figured board photographs so poorly and looks so extraordinary in the hand. Curl, also called fiddleback or flame, comes from fibres that wave up and down in regular ripples perpendicular to the trunk axis, typically two to five waves per centimetre. Sliced across, the alternating end-on and side-on regions produce the familiar bands. Its cause is not fully settled; genetics, growth stress and site conditions all appear to contribute, and it cannot be reliably predicted from a standing tree, which is part of why it commands a premium. Maple, sycamore, ash and cherry show it most often, and the violin trade's demand for it goes back to the sixteenth century. Quilt is a larger-scale, blistered, three-dimensional bubbling most famous in bigleaf maple, produced by broad undulations in the fibre. Birdseye is a scatter of small conical dimples, best known in hard maple, whose cause remains genuinely disputed; theories include dormant bud traces, localised nutrient or hormonal disturbance, and fungal or insect involvement, and no one has yet grown it to order. Burl or burr is a chaotic mass of dormant buds and distorted grain forming a tumour-like growth on a trunk, producing dense clusters of eyes and swirls with essentially no consistent fibre direction, which makes it beautiful, unstable and prone to falling apart under a plane. Crotch or feather figure occurs where a trunk forks and the two sets of fibres interweave under compression, giving the plume seen in walnut and mahogany. Ray fleck, in quartersawn oak and plane, is structural rather than undulatory, being the ray tissue exposed in its own plane. Pommele, ribbon and roey stripe in mahogany, sapele and other tropical species come from interlocked grain, where the tree reverses its spiral direction every few years, so alternate bands face opposite ways and the stripe flips as you walk past it. Spalting is a different phenomenon entirely: the black zone lines are fungal barriers laid down where competing colonies meet in decaying wood. It is decay caught at a useful stage, which means spalted stock is weakened, sometimes punky, and carries spores worth respecting with a mask.

sections.heading: Pores, Texture and Species Identification by Eye
sections.body: Identifying a timber from a small planed sample is a genuine skill, and the reliable route is not colour, which varies wildly with age, light exposure and finish, but the arrangement of pores seen on the end grain. A hand lens of ten to fourteen times magnification and a freshly sliced end-grain surface, pared with a sharp chisel or razor rather than sanded, will settle most questions in under a minute. Hardwoods fall into three groups by pore distribution. Ring-porous species produce a band of large earlywood vessels at the start of each ring and much smaller latewood vessels afterwards, giving a strong visual ring boundary and a coarse, open texture on the face. Oak, ash, elm, chestnut and hickory are ring-porous, and this is why their long open pores hold dirt, need grain filler for a mirror finish, and make them terrible choices for a wine cup unless coopered. Diffuse-porous species scatter vessels evenly through the ring, producing faint boundaries and an even, fine texture. Maple, birch, cherry, poplar, beech and most tropical hardwoods are diffuse-porous, take detail crisply, and finish smooth without filler. Semi-ring-porous species such as walnut and some cherries sit between the two. Softwoods have no vessels at all, only tracheids, so the end grain shows no pores under a lens, just the earlywood-to-latewood density change. The presence or absence of resin canals is the next discriminator: pines, spruces, larches and Douglas fir have them, appearing as small dark specks, while firs, cedars, hemlocks and yew do not. Combined with smell, which is a legitimate diagnostic, cedar, cypress and pine are unmistakable on a fresh cut, this narrows most softwoods quickly. Other usable characters include weight, since density is one of the strongest predictors of behaviour and a small offcut in the hand tells you a great deal; hardness, testable by pressing a thumbnail into a corner; ray height, visible on the end grain as fine lines crossing the rings; and the presence of tyloses, the bubble-like plugs filling the earlywood vessels of white oak but not red oak, which is why white oak is watertight enough for barrels and red oak is not. Blowing gently through a short piece of red oak end-to-end will actually pass air; white oak will not, and this parlour trick is a genuinely definitive test. Two honest cautions. Positive identification to species is often impossible by eye even for specialists, since many timbers are sold under trade names covering several botanical species with different properties. And endangered or restricted timbers, particularly rosewoods and ebonies under CITES regulation, cannot be distinguished from legal substitutes without laboratory work, so provenance paperwork matters more than appearance.

sections.heading: Grain Direction and Machining: Tearout and How To Beat It
sections.body: Tearout is the lifting and levering-out of fibres ahead of a cutting edge, and understanding it converts a maddening surface defect into a controllable variable. When a blade meets fibres that slope up toward the surface, the wedge action of the bevel lifts them, and because wood splits far more easily than it shears, the split runs ahead of the edge and a chunk of fibre tears free below the intended surface. The depth of the damage is roughly proportional to how far the split runs before the edge catches up. Four levers control it, and they can be applied in any combination. The first is direction: cut with the fibres wherever the geometry allows, and simply reversing a board on a jointer or reversing the direction of a hand plane pass solves the majority of cases. Where grain reverses within one board, which is routine in figured stock, direction alone cannot save you. The second is cutting angle. A standard bench plane with a 45-degree bed produces a shaving that lifts and levers. Raising the effective attack angle to 50, 55 or 60 degrees changes the mechanism from splitting to scraping, at the cost of more effort and faster edge dulling. This is achieved by a high-angle frog, a bevel-up plane with a steep blade bevel, or, most cheaply, by honing a small back bevel of 10 to 15 degrees on an ordinary iron. At around 90 degrees you have a scraper, which cannot tear out at all and produces dust and fine shavings rather than continuous ones. The third is chip control. A chipbreaker set very close to the edge, on the order of 0.1 to 0.3 mm, bends the shaving sharply upward the instant it forms and stops the split running ahead. Research at the University of Tokyo in the 1980s, later publicised widely in the 2010s, demonstrated this experimentally with high-speed film, confirming what nineteenth-century plane makers had asserted. On machines the equivalent is a chip breaker bar and pressure bar on a planer or thicknesser, and closing the throat opening of a hand plane serves the same purpose less effectively. The fourth is depth of cut and moisture. Halving the shaving thickness roughly halves the leverage available to lift a fibre, so a series of fine passes beats one heavy one.
